## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
\begin{marginfigure}
\resizebox{0.92\linewidth}{!}{\mlphysicalstackfull{100}{20}{20}{20}{20}}
\end{marginfigure}
:::

_Why can a robot recognize what to do yet still be too late to act?_

Learned models are what let a physical machine handle objects and scenes that no engineer enumerated, and they are also the largest and least predictable computation the machine carries. A model that recognizes the right object still has to move its weights through an onboard processor that sensing and control also depend on, and a larger model that recognizes more takes longer to answer. While it computes, the world keeps moving, so a correct answer can arrive after the conditions that justified it have changed. Predicting a sequence of future motions keeps the actuators supplied between model updates, but it cannot make those motions respond to observations the model has not yet received, and a proposal that arrives on time can still be wrong in ways the model's own confidence does not reveal. An engineer who treats the learned model as a function that returns actions cannot size the processor, set the rates at which proposals are renewed, or say how long the machine may keep moving on an answer that has gone stale. Because motion beyond the causal boundary cannot be recalled, every learned proposal must remain a request that an independent permission path can refuse in time.

{{< pagebreak >}}

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Compare classical analytical pipelines and learned representations on coverage, sensory robustness, and formal verifiability
- Calculate the memory wall bound on a model's fresh-evaluation rate ($f \le B_{\text{mem}} / M_{\text{weights}}$) under the embodied batch size 1 constraint, and explain why weight-only quantization shortens the bandwidth-bound decode but not the compute-bound prefill
- Estimate key-value cache expansion from multi-camera tokenization, hidden dimensions, and retained history windows
- Explain how action chunking ($H$) amortizes off-chip weight transfers over physical wall-clock time without improving closed-loop reaction latency
- Compare autoregressive, one-pass, and iterative action decoders by the sequential evaluations and off-chip transfers one chunk costs
- Apply replanning period, inference latency, and target drift to size an action chunk for a dynamic target
- Evaluate the interface between a slow and a fast proposer by what the permission path can check against its own evidence
- Diagnose cognitive failure modes: semantic hallucinations, uncalibrated softmax overconfidence, perceptual chattering, and expired intent leases
- Identify the trajectory, timestamps, and validity information a proposer must hand to independent real-time verification

:::

## The Embodied Brain {#sec-brain-embodied}

The Brain is the layer of a physical AI system that interprets what the sensors report and proposes what the body should do next. Over the past decade that layer has moved from hand-authored geometry and state machines to learned models, and in particular to vision-language-action models that relate an instruction and a camera image to candidate motion for objects no engineer enumerated. The move puts the machine's most demanding computation on its least predictable path. A learned proposer is large, it shares an onboard processor with sensing and control, and its output describes a world that keeps moving while the model computes. One constraint follows and organizes the rest of this chapter. A learned proposal is useful only if it arrives, and remains true, within the time the physical situation allows, and it stays a proposal, because the permission path below the proposal boundary decides whether it may act. The chapter establishes what a learned proposer costs on a real processor, how that cost fixes the rates at which the machine can renew its proposals, how long each proposal stays valid, and what it must carry for the permission path to check it.

The warehouse mobile manipulator shows the constraint concretely. It can stay within the torque, thermal, voltage, and stopping limits established in @sec-body and still fail to grasp an unfamiliar ceramic mug from a moving conveyor. Those limits describe what the body can sustain. They do not identify the mug's handle or choose a path around a coworker's hand. A learned model can supply that missing interpretation, but the model's output remains a candidate action until the permission path checks it against current evidence and physical limits.

The timing problem begins while the model computes. The mug keeps moving, and the arm still needs feedback to track the motion already admitted. A larger model may improve recognition while taking longer to produce the next proposal. The relevant engineering quantities are therefore distinct: how often the model incorporates a fresh observation, how many future setpoints each proposal contains, and how long its evidence remains useful. Increasing the number of setpoints does not renew the evidence behind them.

The resulting **two-speed brain architecture**\index{Two-speed brain architecture!hybrid control} separates learned deliberation from the real-time permission and tracking path (@fig-two-speed-brain). The Brain proposes a goal or a trajectory; faster control continues below the proposal boundary even when deliberation pauses. Action Chunking Transformers (ACT) [@zhao2023learning] and Diffusion Policies [@chi2024diffusionpolicy] can supply multiple future setpoints in one proposal. The permission path determines which part may execute and when continued execution must end. This division gives learning room to improve task capability without giving an inference delay authority to suspend physical protection.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/spa_locator_p.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="S·P·A locator triad with the Plan node highlighted."}

*The Plan axis: high-capacity neural deliberation emitting unprivileged action chunks.*

```{python}
#| label: brain-two-speed-rates
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ TWO-SPEED RATES (LEGO GUARD FOR A HAND-DRAWN FIGURE)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-two-speed-brain (fig03_two_speed_brain.svg) in the chapter
# │          opening.
# │ Goal:    Print the caption's rates and keep the SVG's hand-drawn labels
# │          equal to the running machine's registry values.
# │ Show:    intent model 2 Hz, 336 ms; chunk renewal 20 Hz, 40 ms inference;
# │          1 kHz permission tick.
# │ How:     Read the registry; check() fails the build if a registry change
# │          leaves the SVG labels stale.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_frequency, fmt_latency, check

class TwoSpeedRates:
    """Registry rates that fig03_two_speed_brain.svg draws as text."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
    f_intent = RM.intent_rate  # category: chosen
    t_intent = RM.intent_inference_latency.to(millisecond)  # category: derived (prefill plus decode)
    f_chunk = RM.chunk_rate  # category: chosen
    t_chunk = RM.chunk_inference_latency.to(millisecond)  # category: illustrative (P99 incl. vision)
    f_tick = RM.permission_rate  # category: chosen

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(f_intent.to(hertz).magnitude - 2.0) < 1e-9, f"SVG draws the intent model at 2 Hz; registry says {f_intent}.")
    check(round(t_intent.magnitude) == 336, f"SVG draws 336 ms per intent evaluation; registry says {t_intent}.")
    check(abs(f_chunk.to(hertz).magnitude - 20.0) < 1e-9, f"SVG draws chunk renewal at 20 Hz; registry says {f_chunk}.")
    check(abs(t_chunk.magnitude - 40.0) < 1e-9, f"SVG draws 40 ms chunk inference; registry says {t_chunk}.")
    check(abs(f_tick.to(hertz).magnitude - 1000.0) < 1e-9, f"SVG draws a 1 kHz permission tick; registry says {f_tick}.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    f_intent_str = fmt_frequency(f_intent, unit=hertz, precision=0)
    f_chunk_str = fmt_frequency(f_chunk, unit=hertz, precision=0)
    f_tick_str = fmt_frequency(f_tick, unit=ureg.kilohertz, precision=0)
```

::: {#fig-two-speed-brain fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Two-speed brain architecture**: Above the proposal boundary, two learned proposers run at their own rates, an intent model at `{python} TwoSpeedRates.f_intent_str` and a chunk policy renewing at `{python} TwoSpeedRates.f_chunk_str`. Below it, the permission path checks each proposal against measured state on a `{python} TwoSpeedRates.f_tick_str` tick, and the drives close their own current and velocity loops. A proposal carries no authority until it is admitted; a refusal returns the proposers to a plan from measured state." fig-alt="Two regions separated by a dashed vertical line labeled proposal boundary. Left region, Brain learned proposers: observations feed an intent model at 2 hertz and 336 milliseconds per evaluation, which passes a goal to a chunk policy at 20 hertz renewal and 40 milliseconds inference; a state resynchronization box below feeds the chunk policy. Right region, Nervous System and Body: encoders and scanner feed a permission path at a 1 kilohertz tick, which sends an admitted command to drives with current and velocity loops, which move the physical plant; the plant feeds back to the encoders. A dashed proposal arrow crosses from the chunk policy to the permission path, and a dashed refusal arrow returns from the permission path to state resynchronization."}
![](images/svg/fig03_two_speed_brain.svg){width="90%"}
:::

A learned proposer earns its place when training gives it useful coverage beyond the hand-authored cases. For the conveyor pick, that means relating the instruction to the visible mug and proposing a graspable region. Recognition still needs measured geometry before it can specify a reachable pose, and robustness to glare or occlusion depends on the operating conditions represented in the evidence. The added capability must fit the processor and the time available to act.

@Fig-cadence-gap places the machine's two learned proposers beside the rates of physical control. The sloped lines are the ceiling that streaming the weights alone imposes on the machine's application processor, derived in @sec-brain-memory-wall. Both proposers run well below that ceiling, because other work in each evaluation also takes time, and neither comes near the permission loop's rate. The design decision is which computation can finish before the current proposal expires; the memory and timing calculations below make that decision concrete for the mobile manipulator.

::: {#fig-cadence-gap fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Cadence regimes on the machine's processor**: The weight-streaming ceiling $f \le B_{\text{sustained}}/M_{\text{weights}}$ on the mobile manipulator's application processor for FP16 and INT4 weights, against parameter count, with the machine's intent model and chunk policy at their chosen rates. The ceiling rules rates out; it does not predict them, because prefill, vision, and decoding add time that weight traffic does not count." fig-alt="Log-log plot of update rate against parameter count. Two parallel descending lines show the FP16 and INT4 weight-streaming ceilings. The chunk policy at 80 million parameters and 20 hertz and the intent model at 7 billion parameters and 2 hertz both sit below their ceilings. Shaded bands mark the permission-loop, chunk, and intent rate ranges."}

```{python}
#| label: fig-cadence-gap
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CADENCE REGIMES ON THE MACHINE'S PROCESSOR (FIGURE)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-cadence-gap, previewing @sec-brain-memory-wall
# │ Goal:    replace anonymous illustrative points with the computed
# │          weight-streaming ceiling and the machine's two proposers
# │ Show:    f_max = B_sustained / M_weights for FP16 and INT4 weights; intent
# │          model (7B, 2 Hz) and ACT chunk policy (80M, 20 Hz) below them
# │ How:     registry bandwidth x dram_efficiency; RM.intent_rate, RM.chunk_rate
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from mlsysim import viz, Embodied
from mlsysim.core.units import GB, second, hertz, param, byte
from mlsysim.fmt import check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

# ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────────────
_b_sus = (RM.brain_soc.memory.bandwidth * RM.dram_efficiency).to(GB / second).magnitude  # derived
_bpp = {"FP16 weights": 2.0, "INT4 weights": RM.intent_weight_bytes_per_param.to(byte / param).magnitude}  # chosen
_intent = (RM.intent_model.parameters.to(param).magnitude, RM.intent_rate.to(hertz).magnitude)
_chunk = (RM.chunk_model.parameters.to(param).magnitude, RM.chunk_rate.to(hertz).magnitude)

# ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
_n = np.logspace(7, 10.5, 200)
_ceiling = {k: _b_sus * 1e9 / (_n * v) for k, v in _bpp.items()}
_intent_wall = _b_sus * 1e9 / (_intent[0] * _bpp["INT4 weights"])
_chunk_wall = _b_sus * 1e9 / (_chunk[0] * 2.0)

# ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
check(_intent[1] < _intent_wall, "Intent rate must sit below its INT4 streaming ceiling")
check(_chunk[1] < _chunk_wall, "Chunk rate must sit below its FP16 streaming ceiling")

# ┌── 5. PLOT ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
fig, ax, COLORS, plt = viz.setup_plot(figsize=(7, 4.5))
ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.axhspan(100, 1000, color="gray", alpha=0.12, label="Permission and servo loops (100–1000 Hz)")
# Vol IV roles: learned proposers in the proposal role (bronze); red is reserved for consequence.
PROPOSAL = "#B87333"
ax.axhspan(10, 50, color="#007A87", alpha=0.08, label="Chunk renewal (10–50 Hz)")
ax.axhspan(1, 5, color="#B87333", alpha=0.08, label="Intent revision (1–5 Hz)")
for (k, f), ls in zip(_ceiling.items(), ["-", "--"]):
    ax.plot(_n, f, ls, color=COLORS["BlueLine"], lw=1.4, label=f"Streaming ceiling, {k}")
ax.plot(*_chunk, "o", ms=9, color=PROPOSAL, zorder=5)
ax.annotate(
    "Chunk policy\n(ACT, 20 Hz)",
    xy=_chunk,
    xytext=(_chunk[0] * 0.18, _chunk[1] * 0.25),
    fontsize=8,
    color=PROPOSAL,
    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=PROPOSAL, lw=0.9),
)
ax.plot(*_intent, "o", ms=9, color=PROPOSAL, zorder=5)
ax.annotate(
    "Intent model\n(INT4, 2 Hz)",
    xy=_intent,
    xytext=(_intent[0] * 0.05, _intent[1] * 0.3),
    fontsize=8,
    color=PROPOSAL,
    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=PROPOSAL, lw=0.9),
)
ax.set_xlim(1e7, 3e10)
ax.set_ylim(0.3, 3e4)
ax.set_xlabel("Parameter count (log scale)")
ax.set_ylabel("Update rate [Hz] (log scale)")
plt.legend(bbox_to_anchor=(1.02, 1), loc="upper left", frameon=False, fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
plt.close()
```

:::

@Sec-brain-classical-wall shows why pipelines built on hand-authored geometry and state machines lose coverage outside the factory cell, and @sec-brain-learned-representations shows what learned representations recover and what they cost in tokens and memory traffic. @Sec-brain-cognitive-pipeline turns that cost into the machine's numbers: the memory wall that bounds how often its intent model can run and the quantization that eases it, the action chunking that keeps the arm supplied between evaluations, the drift that bounds how long each chunk stays true, and the interface through which the intent model hands a checkable target to the chunk policy. @Sec-brain-cognitive-vulnerabilities then takes up the ways a proposal can arrive on time and still be wrong, each of which leaves the permission path with a proposal it must be able to refuse.

## The Classical Wall {#sec-brain-classical-wall}

A gripper in a fixed workcell can approach the same fixture along the same path on every cycle. Engineers can describe that task through geometry, equations of motion, and explicit transitions between stages. Classical control and robotics build on this analytical approach [@wiener1948cybernetics; @kalman1960new; @craig2005introduction]. The difficulty for the conveyor mug is extending the description to objects and conditions that the engineer did not enumerate.

Analytical kinematics and dynamics map desired end-effector[^fn-hw-end-effector] motion into joint motion and actuator torque.[^fn-math-classical-dynamics] Perception can match measured geometry against a known computer-aided design (CAD) model, while a state machine advances through approaching, aligning, grasping, and retracting. In a calibrated workcell these components solve a bounded task with explicit assumptions. Their computational cost and timing still depend on the chosen algorithm, processor, and contact model.

[^fn-hw-end-effector]: **End-Effector**\index{End-effector!definition}: The active tool, gripper, or hand at the distal tip of a robotic manipulator that interacts directly with physical workpieces and the environment.

[^fn-math-classical-dynamics]: **Rigid-Body Dynamics Formulation**\index{Rigid-body dynamics!Euler-Lagrange formulation}\index{Equations of motion!manipulator dynamics}: Classical control computes generalized torques via the standard manipulator equation $\mathbf{M}(\mathbf{q})\ddot{\mathbf{q}} + \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{q}, \dot{\mathbf{q}})\dot{\mathbf{q}} + \mathbf{g}(\mathbf{q}) = \boldsymbol{\tau}$, where $\mathbf{M}(\mathbf{q})$ represents the configuration-dependent inertia matrix, $\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{q}, \dot{\mathbf{q}})$ captures Coriolis and centripetal terms, and $\mathbf{g}(\mathbf{q})$ accounts for gravitational loading. Specifically, $\mathbf{M}(\mathbf{q})$ captures configuration-dependent mass moments: extending an articulated linkage shifts mass outward from the rotational axes, increasing reflected rotational inertia ($I \propto m r^2$) and demanding quadratically higher joint torque for equivalent angular acceleration. Unmodeled frictional contacts, fluid drag, or deformable objects can make this rigid-body model inaccurate; accounting for those effects can also increase the computational cost. Derivations are provided in @sec-appendix-control.

::: {#fig-industrial-welding fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Industrial spot-welding workcell**: Multiple six-degree-of-freedom articulated robots execute preprogrammed spot welding paths on stamped automotive chassis at the BMW Leipzig plant. Operating in a calibrated factory environment with submillimeter repeatable fixtures and safety interlock cages, classical controllers provide deterministic cycle timing and formal stability proofs. (Credit: BMW Werk Leipzig, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:BMW_Leipzig_MEDIA_050719_Download_Karosseriebau_max.jpg), CC BY-SA 2.0 DE.)" fig-alt="Articulated industrial robots executing automated spot welding on an automotive chassis within a safety-caged factory cell."}
![](images/jpg/fig03_real_industrial_welding.jpg){width="85%"}
:::

Where the operational environment is strictly structured and bounded (@fig-industrial-welding), classical methods provide dependable behavior within their modeled conditions. On an automated automotive assembly line, an industrial robot welds stamped steel panels where every workpiece arrives at an exact coordinate within sub-millimeter tolerances. Ambient lighting is tightly regulated by industrial fixtures, and human workers are excluded by physical interlock safety fences. Within the causal boundary defined in @sec-boundary-causal-boundary, this controlled regime permits explicit models, bounded servo timing, and formal Lyapunov stability analysis under stated assumptions. Engineers can verify trajectory tracking error bounds ($\lVert \mathbf{e}(t) \rVert \le \epsilon$) and certify controller software coverage against safety standards without collecting empirical demonstrations.

Yet when an embodied machine leaves the structured factory cage to operate in unstructured open-world environments (@fig-unstructured-rescue), this analytical paradigm hits the **classical wall** [@brooks1991intelligence; @levine2018learning]. The physical world is not a sterile CAD drawing; it is continuous, deformable, and endlessly variable.

::: {#fig-unstructured-rescue fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Unstructured search-and-rescue robot**: A four-wheeled rescue robot carrying cameras and a laser scanner on a pan-tilt mast works through a test arena of tilted ramps and narrow openings, with a victim dummy placed on a high shelf. In such unmapped environments, preauthored geometric models and rigid state machines can lose coverage; learned policies may help infer spatial affordances and traversability from sensory streams. (Credit: Hector, Technische Universität Darmstadt, at the 2010 RoboCup German Open; photo by Mike1024, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:RoboCup_Rescue_robot_Hector_from_Darmstadt_at_2010_German_open.jpg), public domain.)" fig-alt="Four-wheeled robot with a sensor mast on tilted plywood ramps in a rescue test arena, seen through a round cutout, with a doll on a shelf in the background."}
![](images/jpg/fig03_real_unstructured_rescue.jpg){width="85%"}
:::

Outside that workcell, the same pipeline must cope with object variation, imperfect sensing, and unexpected task states. A CAD template does not cover every deformation of a garment; glare can erase the depth edge separating two packages; and an unexpected hand can invalidate a preauthored transition from approach to grasp. Adding templates, thresholds, and branches extends coverage, but each addition requires engineering and validation for the new conditions.

Learning offers a different way to obtain that coverage. Training can associate varied observations with useful object features and demonstrated behavior without requiring a separate geometric template for every instance. This does not replace the analytical controller that tracks a proposed motion. It adds a computationally demanding interpretation stage whose memory traffic and latency must fit above that controller.

## Learned Representations {#sec-brain-learned-representations}

Asked to take the unfamiliar ceramic mug from the conveyor, a learned model can relate the instruction to a visible handle and propose a grasp region without an exact CAD template. Vision-language-action (VLA) models combine images, language, and robot state to produce candidate actions [@brohan2023rt1; @brohan2023rt2; @kim2024openvla]. They descend from embodied language models such as PaLM-E, which emitted language plans rather than motor commands [@driess2023palme]. Their value is the coverage obtained from training across objects and conditions, rather than a guarantee that any unfamiliar scene will be interpreted correctly.

Demonstrations can also teach coordinated behavior for tasks whose contacts and deformations are difficult to specify completely, such as routing a cable with two arms (@fig-aloha-manipulator) [@zhao2023learning; @chi2024diffusionpolicy]. Learned sensory features may tolerate variations represented in that training, while a controller still needs measured geometry and physical limits to execute the proposal. Task success under tested conditions supplies evidence of capability; it does not establish behavior under every lighting change, contact, or payload.

The systems cost follows from how that capability is represented. Images become model inputs, retained context occupies memory, and the model must compute a new action before its observations become stale. The useful comparison with a classical pipeline therefore includes both task coverage and the cost of renewing a proposal.

::: {#fig-aloha-manipulator fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Bimanual teleoperation workcell**: Dual-arm teleoperation setup featuring two six-degree-of-freedom follower arms, two leader arms for kinesthetic teleoperation, multi-view cameras (overhead and wrist-mounted), and parallel grippers mounted to an extruded aluminum frame. The physical AI policy ingests synchronized multi-camera streams to predict continuous end-effector trajectories, and the permission path must refuse any proposal that would cause self-collision or motor over-torquing during closed-loop execution. (Credit: ALOHA 2 Team, ALOHA 2: An Enhanced Low-Cost Hardware for Bimanual Teleoperation, arXiv:2405.02292, CC BY 4.0.)" fig-alt="Dual-arm robotic teleoperation workstation with leader and follower arms, overhead cameras, and grippers mounted on an aluminum frame."}
![](images/png/fig03_real_aloha_manipulator.png){width="85%"}
:::

::: {#fig-vla-architecture fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Embodied Vision-Language-Action (VLA) architecture**: A representative dataflow. (1) Camera patches receive 2D image-position and camera identifiers alongside language and robot-state tokens; metric depth still requires calibrated evidence. (2) Self-attention mixes the combined token sequence; the colored grid illustrates internal attention weights, not a verified affordance or grasp pose. (3) Autoregressive token decoders emit tokens sequentially, whereas one-pass chunk heads and iterative action experts generate candidate multi-step chunks ($\mathbf{A}_{t:t+H-1}$) in one pass or over several refinement steps. (4) An independent permission path checks candidate motion against sensed state and modeled limits before actuation. (Synthesized from Brohan et al. [@brohan2023rt1; @brohan2023rt2], Kim et al. [@kim2024openvla], and Octo Model Team [@octo_2023])." fig-alt="Comprehensive architectural schematic of a Vision-Language-Action foundation model showing spatial patch slicing, 2D positional embeddings, multimodal self-attention weights in an illustrative image grid, discrete vs. continuous action decoders, and an independent proposal boundary."}
![](images/svg/fig03_vla_architecture.svg){width="100%"}

```{python}
#| label: calc-brain-state-of-practice
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ PUBLISHED VLA AND DUAL-SYSTEM FIGURES (STATE OF PRACTICE, AS OF 2026)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: item 3 of @sec-brain-learned-representations, the decoder-family
# │          paragraphs of @sec-brain-action-chunking, @tbl-03-state-of-practice
# │ Goal:    hold every published 2023-2025 system figure the chapter quotes in
# │          one place, each with its source, so the dated table can be refreshed
# │          without touching the argument
# │ Show:    horizons (DP 16/8, pi0 50, ACT 100); OFT 26x; FAST 30-60 tokens;
# │          Helix, GR00T N1, Gemini Robotics rates
# │ How:     literature values, each verified against the paper on 2026-09-29;
# │          promotion candidates for mlsysim literature/registry
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_int, fmt_params, fmt_frequency, fmt_latency, fmt_multiple, fmt_percent, fmt_memory, check

class StateOfPractice:
    """Published architecture figures, verified against each source (2026-09-29)."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    # Chi et al. 2024 (Diffusion Policy): prediction horizon T_p and executed T_a
    dp_predict, dp_execute = 16, 8  # category: literature
    # Zhao et al. 2023 (ACT): chunk size k = 100 at 50 Hz
    act_k = 100  # category: literature
    act_rate = 50 * hertz  # category: literature (ACT control rate)
    # Black et al. 2024 (pi0), Sec. IV and App. A-D
    pi0_params = 3.3e9 * param  # category: literature (total)
    pi0_expert = 300e6 * param  # category: literature (action expert)
    pi0_h = 50  # category: literature
    pi0_steps = 10  # category: literature (flow integration steps)
    pi0_rate = 50 * hertz  # category: literature ("up to 50 Hz")
    pi0_latency = 73 * millisecond  # category: literature (on-board, RTX 4090)
    # Kim et al. 2024 (OpenVLA): about 6 Hz on one RTX 4090 in bfloat16
    openvla_rate = 6 * hertz  # category: literature
    # Kim, Finn, Liang 2025 (OpenVLA-OFT): LIBERO, A100, 8-step chunks
    oft_hz, openvla_hz_a100, oft_chunk = 109.7 * hertz, 4.2 * hertz, 8  # category: literature
    # Pertsch et al. 2025 (FAST): 30-60 tokens per chunk; pi0-FAST ~750 ms vs pi0 ~100 ms (RTX 4090)
    fast_tok_lo, fast_tok_hi = 30, 60  # category: literature
    fast_naive, fast_tok_50hz = 700, 53  # category: literature (shirt fold, 50 Hz, Table I)
    fast_task_rate = 50 * hertz  # category: literature (shirt-fold control rate, Table I)
    fast_latency, flow_latency = 750 * millisecond, 100 * millisecond  # category: literature (approximate)
    # Figure AI 2025 (Helix)
    helix_s2_params, helix_s1_params = 7e9 * param, 80e6 * param  # category: literature
    helix_s2_lo, helix_s2_hi, helix_s1_rate = 7 * hertz, 9 * hertz, 200 * hertz  # category: literature
    helix_dof = 35  # category: literature
    # Bjorck et al. 2025 (GR00T N1)
    gr00t_params, gr00t_vlm = 2.2e9 * param, 1.34e9 * param  # category: literature
    gr00t_s2_rate, gr00t_s1_rate = 10 * hertz, 120 * hertz  # category: literature
    gr00t_h, gr00t_steps = 16, 4  # category: literature
    gr00t_latency = 63.9 * millisecond  # category: literature (16-action chunk, L40, bf16)
    # Gemini Robotics Team 2025 (Gemini Robotics): cloud backbone plus on-robot decoder
    gemini_backbone = 160 * millisecond  # category: literature (upper bound, "under 160 ms")
    gemini_e2e = 250 * millisecond  # category: literature ("approximately 250 ms")
    gemini_rate = 50 * hertz  # category: literature (effective control rate with chunks)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    oft_speedup = (oft_hz / openvla_hz_a100).to("dimensionless").magnitude
    fast_ratio = fast_naive / fast_tok_50hz

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(oft_speedup - 26.1) < 0.05, f"OFT speedup drifted: {oft_speedup}")
    check(abs(fast_ratio - 13.2) < 0.05, f"FAST compression drifted: {fast_ratio}")
    check(dp_execute < dp_predict < pi0_h < act_k, "Horizon ordering drifted")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    dp_predict_str, dp_execute_str, act_k_str = fmt_int(dp_predict), fmt_int(dp_execute), fmt_int(act_k)
    act_rate_str = fmt_frequency(act_rate, unit=hertz, precision=0)
    pi0_params_str = fmt_params(pi0_params, precision=1)
    pi0_expert_str = fmt_params(pi0_expert, precision=0)
    pi0_h_str, pi0_steps_str = fmt_int(pi0_h), fmt_int(pi0_steps)
    pi0_rate_str = fmt_frequency(pi0_rate, unit=hertz, precision=0)
    pi0_latency_str = fmt_latency(pi0_latency, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    openvla_rate_str = fmt_frequency(openvla_rate, unit=hertz, precision=0)
    oft_hz_str = fmt_frequency(oft_hz, unit=hertz, precision=1)
    openvla_hz_a100_str = fmt_frequency(openvla_hz_a100, unit=hertz, precision=1)
    oft_chunk_str = fmt_int(oft_chunk)
    oft_speedup_mult_str = fmt_multiple(round(oft_speedup), precision=0)  # the paper reports "26x"
    fast_tok_lo_str, fast_tok_hi_str = fmt_int(fast_tok_lo), fmt_int(fast_tok_hi)
    fast_naive_str, fast_tok_50hz_str = fmt_int(fast_naive), fmt_int(fast_tok_50hz)
    fast_ratio_mult_str = fmt_multiple(fast_ratio, precision=1)
    fast_task_rate_str = fmt_frequency(fast_task_rate, unit=hertz, precision=0)
    fast_latency_str = fmt_latency(fast_latency, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    flow_latency_str = fmt_latency(flow_latency, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    helix_s2_params_str = fmt_params(helix_s2_params, precision=0)
    helix_s1_params_str = fmt_params(helix_s1_params, precision=0)
    helix_s2_lo_num_str = fmt_int(helix_s2_lo.magnitude)
    helix_s2_hi_str = fmt_frequency(helix_s2_hi, unit=hertz, precision=0)
    helix_s1_rate_str = fmt_frequency(helix_s1_rate, unit=hertz, precision=0)
    helix_dof_str = fmt_int(helix_dof)
    gr00t_params_str = fmt_params(gr00t_params, precision=1)
    gr00t_vlm_str = fmt_params(gr00t_vlm, precision=2)
    gr00t_s2_rate_str = fmt_frequency(gr00t_s2_rate, unit=hertz, precision=0)
    gr00t_s1_rate_str = fmt_frequency(gr00t_s1_rate, unit=hertz, precision=0)
    gr00t_h_str, gr00t_steps_str = fmt_int(gr00t_h), fmt_int(gr00t_steps)
    gr00t_latency_str = fmt_latency(gr00t_latency, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    gemini_backbone_str = fmt_latency(gemini_backbone, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    gemini_e2e_str = fmt_latency(gemini_e2e, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    gemini_rate_str = fmt_frequency(gemini_rate, unit=hertz, precision=0)
```

For the mug pick, the model must turn images and instructions into a candidate motion. The dataflow in @fig-vla-architecture separates that computation into input encoding, a shared representation, and an action decoder, followed by the handoff to independent permission. A token is a vector representing part of an input, such as an image patch; the backbone combines those vectors, and the decoder turns the combined representation into proposed actions. The engineering comparison below follows what each stage stores, transfers, and delivers:

1. **Sensory Ingestion and Spatial Tokenization (The Inputs):**
   A vision transformer (ViT) frontend slices each incoming camera frame into a grid of non-overlapping pixel patches of size $P \times P$ (typically $14 \times 14$ or $16 \times 16$ pixels). Each patch is linearly projected into a vector of width $d$, augmented with a position embedding (learned in the SigLIP and DINOv2 encoders that OpenVLA uses [@kim2024openvla], sinusoidal in some other designs), and tagged with a learned camera identifier.

   In an illustrative three-camera configuration (left wrist, right wrist, and an overhead torso mount) capturing $224 \times 224$ images, the image frontend prepares a buffer for each view. Each frame yields $(224 / 14)^2 = 256$ spatial patches. Across three cameras, ingestion injects $3 \times 256 = 768$ visual tokens into the model's sequence on every perceptual step. When concatenated with tokenized natural language commands ($\sim 32$ tokens) and proprioceptive joint state embeddings ($\sim 16$ tokens), the initial context sequence length exceeds $S \approx 800$ tokens. In 16-bit floating-point (FP16) precision ($2\,\text{bytes}$ per element) with hidden dimension $d = 4096$, the initial token embedding matrix alone occupies:
   $$M_{\text{embed}} = S \times d \times 2\,\text{bytes} = 800 \times 4096 \times 2 \approx 6.55\,\text{MB}$$
   Crucially, 2D image coordinates and internal attention patterns do not constitute metric depth: projecting an end-effector into physical 3D space requires calibrated extrinsic camera matrices and depth telemetry.

2. **Multimodal Alignment and Attention (The Backbone):**
   For the illustrative backbone, the token sequence passes through $L = 32$ transformer layers where standard multi-head self-attention computes pairwise token interactions. The cache estimate below assumes full-width keys and values in every layer. While full self-attention incurs quadratic computational complexity ($O(S^2 d)$ FLOPs), at the systems level the Key-Value (KV) cache that retains prior token states for autoregressive context expands linearly ($O(L \cdot S \cdot d)$):
   $$M_{\text{KV}} = 2 \times L \times d \times S \times \text{bytes}$$
   For a 32-layer model with $d = 4096$ using FP16 storage, each context token claims $2 \times 32 \times 4096 \times 2 = 524{,}288\,\text{bytes} \approx 0.524\,\text{MB}$ of KV cache. Reading this KV cache across off-chip DRAM on every token step creates massive memory bus traffic that directly competes with weight streaming. An observation step of several hundred tokens therefore holds hundreds of megabytes of KV state, which the two-proposer notebook computes for the machine. Because memory bus access under Unified Memory Architecture (UMA) is a shared zero-sum resource, rereading that state risks starving real-time sensor direct memory access (DMA) buffers. Single-observation VLAs such as OpenVLA rebuild their context from each new frame and carry no cache across control steps; only designs that condition on retained history pay this cost repeatedly. Grouped-query attention (GQA) reduces key-value width by sharing keys and values across query heads; cross-attention can instead limit which retained representations the decoder reads. The saving depends on the architecture and is not implied by action chunking. Furthermore, strong attention weights between language tokens (such as "mug handle") and visual patches do not prove geometric affordance or collision-free clearance; nor does the KV cache track object permanence during physical occlusions. The formal patch-embedding, position-encoding, and attention formulations appear in @sec-appendix-ml-patch-embedding.

3. **Specialized Action Decoders (The Outputs):**
   Instead of generating open-ended conversational text, the final hidden representation $\mathbf{h}_{\text{context}} \in \mathbb{R}^d$ is routed to specialized action decoders. While vision-language navigation (VLN) models emit topological waypoints or heading rates $(v_t, \omega_t)$ (@fig-vln-navigation), manipulation (VLA) models diverge sharply in how they bridge semantic representations to physical motion:

   Discrete action decoders map each action dimension to a categorical token by dividing its range into bins [@brohan2023rt1; @brohan2023rt2; @kim2024openvla]. Autoregressive decoders such as RT-2 and OpenVLA then generate those tokens one after another, one model evaluation per action dimension [@brohan2023rt2; @kim2024openvla]. Discretization does not require sequential decoding. RT-1 emits all of its action tokens from one pass, and its authors found that conditioning each token on the previous ones did not improve performance and more than doubled inference time [@brohan2023rt1].

   What separates the decoders in current use is how many model evaluations one chunk of future actions costs and which weights each evaluation rereads. Three families cover practice as of 2026:

   * *Autoregressive tokens.* Each token costs one evaluation. With one token per action dimension per step, a chunk of $H$ steps with $d_a$ values each costs $H d_a$ sequential evaluations, so latency grows with both. Per-step binning also fails at high control rates, because consecutive tokens become nearly identical and give next-token training little to learn from. FAST (frequency-space action sequence tokenization) compresses the chunk instead: it applies a discrete cosine transform to each action dimension over the chunk, rewriting that dimension's trajectory as a sum of cosine waves of rising frequency, so that a smooth motion needs only a few nonzero low-frequency weights. It then rounds those weights and merges frequently repeated runs of them into single tokens with byte-pair encoding, the compression step text tokenizers use, so the token count follows the chunk's information content rather than $H d_a$. On a `{python} StateOfPractice.fast_task_rate_str` task it cut `{python} StateOfPractice.fast_naive_str` binned tokens to `{python} StateOfPractice.fast_tok_50hz_str`, a `{python} StateOfPractice.fast_ratio_mult_str` reduction [@pertsch2025fast]. Decoding is still sequential: its authors report about `{python} StateOfPractice.fast_latency_str` per chunk for the FAST version of $\pi_0$, against about `{python} StateOfPractice.flow_latency_str` for the flow version on the same desktop GPU.
   * *One-pass chunk heads.* ACT regresses a whole chunk from one decoder pass [@zhao2023learning]. OpenVLA-OFT gives an autoregressive VLA the same shape by feeding placeholder action embeddings through bidirectional attention and regressing continuous values for every action at once, which raised throughput `{python} StateOfPractice.oft_speedup_mult_str` on `{python} StateOfPractice.oft_chunk_str`-step chunks [@kim2025openvlaoft]. A head trained to regress one answer can average two demonstrated routes into a path through the obstacle between them [@chi2024diffusionpolicy]; ACT's conditional variational autoencoder is one mitigation.
   * *Iterative action experts.* Diffusion Policy removes noise from a candidate chunk over several passes [@chi2024diffusionpolicy]. $\pi_0$ attaches a `{python} StateOfPractice.pi0_expert_str`-parameter flow-matching **action expert**\index{Action expert!flow matching} to a pretrained vision-language model: the backbone reads the observation once and caches its keys and values, and the expert integrates the chunk over `{python} StateOfPractice.pi0_steps_str` steps while attending to that cache, `{python} StateOfPractice.pi0_params_str` parameters in all [@black2024pi0]. Integration here has its freshman-calculus meaning. The expert starts from a chunk of random noise and, at each step, predicts a velocity that points from the current sample toward a demonstrated chunk; moving the sample a small distance along that velocity and repeating is Euler integration, and after the last step the sample is the proposed chunk. Each step is one pass of the expert that rereads the expert's weights and the cached keys and values, not the backbone. $\pi_{0.5}$ and GR00T N1 use the same pattern [@black2025pi05; @bjorck2025gr00t], and $\pi_{0.5}$ trains its backbone on FAST tokens while acting through the flow expert.

   Whatever the family, the continuous output is a trajectory chunk:
   $$\mathbf{A}_{t:t+H-1} = [\mathbf{a}_t, \mathbf{a}_{t+1}, \dots, \mathbf{a}_{t+H-1}] \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times d_a}$$
   Here $H$ counts future setpoints and $d_a$ counts values per action. Published horizons range from tens to about a hundred setpoints: Diffusion Policy predicts `{python} StateOfPractice.dp_predict_str` and executes `{python} StateOfPractice.dp_execute_str` [@chi2024diffusionpolicy], $\pi_0$ predicts `{python} StateOfPractice.pi0_h_str` [@black2024pi0], and ACT predicts `{python} StateOfPractice.act_k_str` at `{python} StateOfPractice.act_rate_str` [@zhao2023learning]. That split between a predicted and an executed horizon returns in @sec-brain-two-proposers as the difference between a supply buffer and permission. A chunk supplies several requested motions from one sensory context; it does not contain new observations. @Sec-brain-action-chunking prices the three families on the machine's processor, and @sec-appendix-ml-multimodal derives discrete tokenization and explains how generative decoders represent alternative demonstrated routes without averaging them into an obstacle.

4. **The Proposal Boundary (Isolation from Actuators):**
   Whether the model is a VLN mobility planner or a VLA manipulation policy, its output is a candidate proposal ($p_t$) on the unprivileged side of the proposal boundary (\ref{dfn-boundary-proposal-boundary}).\index{Unprivileged proposal!proposal boundary} Under the machine model of @sec-boundary-machine-model, the foundation model runs in user space on the application processor and has no path to the pulse-width modulation (PWM) registers or to the current in the motor coils.

   The Brain hands over candidate motion together with the time of the observations that support it. Faster downstream loops track admitted setpoints and regulate motor current using current measurements. A long neural inference cannot suspend those loops or renew old evidence. @Sec-brain-memory-wall prices one fresh evaluation, @sec-nervous-deterministic-fieldbuses prices the path from the processor to the drives, and @sec-nervous-invariant-checking develops the independent checking responsibility.

   Proposals reach the permission path through the handoff of @sec-nervous, and the permission path can refuse a hallucinated proposal when independent measurements, modeled limits, and a feasible fallback support that decision.[^fn-math-unprivileged-control]

[^fn-math-unprivileged-control]: **Proposal Boundary**\index{Proposal boundary!unprivileged proposals}: Treating the neural policy as an unprivileged proposal generator isolates stochastic inference from actuator registers. Candidate trajectory setpoints $\mathbf{q}_{\text{ref}}(t)$ are checked on dedicated safety silicon, so proposals that violate modeled actuator limits or keep-out regions can be rejected before any reaches a drive (@sec-nervous-actuation-authority).

::: {#fig-vln-navigation fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Topological vision-language navigation**: Embodied navigation architecture executing natural-language spatial instructions. Panoramic visual observations are encoded into perceptual tokens, matched against prompt embeddings, and cross-referenced with a dynamically updated topological navigation graph. The action decoder prunes unreachable nodes and emits metric waypoint offsets $(\Delta x, \Delta y)$ and heading setpoints to guide the chassis along traversable semantic frontiers without requiring an exact geometric prior map. (Adapted from An et al. [@an2023etpnav], arXiv:2304.03047, CC BY 4.0.)" fig-alt="Schematic of topological vision-language navigation showing panoramic observation tokens, topological graph matching, and decoded waypoint offsets and heading setpoints."}
![](images/png/fig03_real_vln_topological_navigation.png){width="95%"}
:::

The representation and decoder determine which data each evaluation must touch. A decoder that retains token history pays for its cache, and a backbone whose weights do not remain on chip pays for new off-chip transfers. These costs make the architecture choice concrete: the mobile manipulator needs both useful task interpretation and timely renewal of motion proposals, but need not assign them to the same model.

## Supply, Freshness, and the Memory Wall {#sec-brain-cognitive-pipeline}

At the pick station the mobile manipulator's arm consumes a new setpoint every few tens of milliseconds, while the mug keeps moving along the conveyor. The selected architecture assigns task interpretation to a large, slower intent model and trajectory renewal to a smaller action-chunk policy. Both propose; a separate real-time path checks and tracks admitted motion. We can test that split by pricing a full weight sweep, comparing it with the required renewal period, and then checking the motion buffer against target drift. The single large-model examples below are alternatives used to expose the trade-off, not changes to the selected machine.

After ingestion (the tokenization of @sec-brain-learned-representations), four stages turn those tokens into proposals (@fig-cognitive-pipeline), and Part III develops each one. Here they matter only for what each hands downstream and how quickly that goes stale.

Perception grounds what it recognizes in metric coordinates relative to the base, so that the mug has a 3D position and orientation (an $SE(3)$ pose) and a graspable handle rather than an abstract semantic label;[^fn-brain-metric-grounding] its output ages from the moment of capture, and @sec-perception turns that age into a contract. Memory carries those estimates through occlusion and must let each one expire when the evidence behind it does (@sec-memory). Intent decomposes a task such as "take the ceramic mug off the conveyor and hand it to the coworker at the packing station" into subgoals, and because the mug moves while the intent model deliberates, it hands the planner a target that expires. Planning converts that target into candidate setpoints for the base and the arm, the proposals the permission path will judge (@sec-planning).

The book calls authority that lapses unless it is renewed a lease\index{Lease!authority that lapses}, and two kinds appear in this chapter. The expiring target is an intent lease\index{Intent lease!temporal contract}: it names a grounded target, never a path, and expires at the earliest of its evidence horizon and the deadlines the permission path sets (@sec-intent-lease). The motion the smaller chunk policy proposes runs under a chunk lease\index{Chunk lease!first use}, the longest an admitted chunk may keep driving the actuators without an admitted successor, which @sec-nervous sizes against the stopping budget.

These stages, and the ingestion before them, all run on the application processor and draw on the same memory bus, which is where the machine's cadence is decided. The memory bandwidth, arithmetic, and power of that processor are the physical wall of @sec-boundary-bedrock-laws, and the rest of this section measures what the wall costs each proposer.

[^fn-brain-metric-grounding]: **Metric Spatial Grounding**\index{Metric spatial grounding}\index{Special Euclidean group!SE(3) grounding}: While disembodied AI operates over discrete semantic tokens, physical AI must ground those semantics in the Special Euclidean group $SE(3)$, mapping entities to metric distances (meters) and spatial orientations (quaternions) relative to the robot's base coordinate frame. Failing to maintain this metric grounding causes neural policies to emit kinematically impossible Cartesian paths that breach actuator workspace boundaries.

::: {#fig-cognitive-pipeline fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**The physical AI cognitive flow**: The learned stages run on the application processor and each hands the next a record that ages: ingestion produces tokens, perception a metric pose with its age, memory a belief with its evidence epoch, intent an intent lease, and planning candidate setpoints. Everything up to planning is proposal. Only the permission path, on its own `{python} TwoSpeedRates.f_tick_str` tick across the proposal boundary, can turn a proposal into an admitted command for the drives." fig-alt="Two rows of boxes. Top row: sensors (cameras, IMU, encoders) feed ingestion (hands on tokens), which feeds perception (hands on pose plus age), which feeds memory (hands on belief plus epoch). An arrow wraps from memory down to the second row: intent (hands on intent lease) feeds planning (hands on candidate setpoints). The learned stages sit inside a dashed region labeled application processor. A dashed proposal arrow from planning crosses a vertical dashed line labeled proposal boundary into a permission path box (safety MCU, 1 kHz tick), which sends an admitted command to drives and plant."}
![](images/svg/fig03_cognitive_pipeline_horizontal.svg){width="100%"}
:::

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ High-throughput neural inference accelerators are isolated from deterministic cores in @sec-placement-two-paths-one-die.
:::

On an edge robotics system-on-chip (SoC) with unified memory, model weights, sensor transfers, and host computation share memory bandwidth. A policy cannot budget the full bus for itself while assuming that new camera frames arrive without interference. The transfer bound below is therefore a lower bound on evaluation time; the worked comparison later uses an assumed sustained fraction of peak bandwidth. @Sec-placement-resource-contention develops the allocation and loaded tests needed to establish that supply on a shared processor.

### The memory wall {#sec-brain-memory-wall}

When each evaluation streams weights that cannot remain on-chip, memory bandwidth can limit the update cadence of an embodied neural policy even when arithmetic capacity is available. The **memory wall**\index{Memory wall!physical inference} describes the limit imposed when operands cannot reach arithmetic units fast enough to use their available throughput. In physical AI, the consequence is a delayed proposal while the body continues moving.

On-chip static RAM (SRAM) and caches can reuse weights and intermediate state without another external transfer, but only while the working set fits the memory available to that workload. Off-chip LPDDR5 provides much greater capacity through a narrower shared interface. Cache sizes, access latency, and attainable bandwidth depend on the particular processor and allocation; nominal chip-wide capacity does not establish that an action head will remain resident.

```{python}
#| label: calc-brain-intent-model-latency
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ INTENT-MODEL LATENCY: MEMORY WALL PLUS PREFILL
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: nbk-brain-intent-model-latency (canonical memory-wall example),
# │          @fig-patterson-roofline, and the two-proposer notebook
# │ Goal:    price one fresh intent-model evaluation from both roofline terms
# │          and show which rate the machine can state
# │ Show:    98.04 ms FP16 sweep (10.2 Hz wall); 188.5 ms compute-bound prefill
# │          of S = 288 tokens; 6 decode sweeps; FP16 total 777 ms; INT4 total
# │          336 ms (2.98 Hz) against the 336 ms Jetson measurement; 2 Hz rate
# │ How:     calc_vla_inference_latency (prefill max(F/(u Pi), sweep) plus
# │          (D - 1) bandwidth-bound decode sweeps); RM.intent_latency_breakdown
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import (
    fmt_params,
    fmt_memory,
    fmt_bandwidth,
    fmt_latency,
    fmt_frequency,
    fmt_percent,
    fmt_int,
    fmt_qty,
    fmt_arithmetic_intensity,
    fmt_display_math,
    sci_latex,
    check,
)

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

class IntentModelLatency:
    """One fresh intent-model evaluation: FP16 memory wall, prefill, decode, INT4."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    model = RM.intent_model  # category: chosen (OpenVLA-sized intent model)
    soc = RM.brain_soc  # category: datasheet (application processor)
    n_params = model.parameters  # category: datasheet
    n_layers = model.layers  # category: datasheet
    d_model = model.hidden_dim  # category: datasheet
    d_action = model.action_dim  # category: datasheet (one token per action dimension)
    s_in = RM.intent_input_tokens  # category: illustrative (256 patches derived + 32 prompt)
    patches = 256  # category: derived; (224 / 14)^2 patches for one 224 x 224 view
    pi_fp16 = soc.compute.precision_flops["fp16"]  # category: datasheet (dense FP16 GPU)
    b_peak = soc.memory.bandwidth  # category: datasheet
    eta = RM.dram_efficiency  # category: illustrative (sustained fraction of peak)
    u = RM.intent_compute_utilization  # category: illustrative (achieved fraction of FP16 peak)
    bpp_fp16 = 2 * (byte / param)  # category: chosen (FP16 weights)
    bpp_int4 = RM.intent_weight_bytes_per_param  # category: chosen (INT4 weights, deployed)
    t_measured = RM.intent_reference_latency  # category: measured (Jetson AI Lab, INT4 on AGX Orin)
    s_three_cameras = 800  # category: illustrative; three views plus prompt and state tokens

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    m_fp16 = memory_from_params(n_params, bpp_fp16)
    m_int4 = RM.intent_weight_memory
    b_sus = (b_peak * eta).to(GB / second)
    ridge = (pi_fp16 / b_peak).to(flop / byte)
    intensity_prefill = (2 * n_params.to(count).magnitude * s_in * flop / (m_fp16)).to(flop / byte)

    fp16 = calc_vla_inference_latency(
        n_params,
        m_fp16,
        s_in,
        d_action,
        pi_fp16,
        b_peak,
        bus_efficiency=eta,
        compute_utilization=u,
        n_layers=n_layers,
        hidden_dim=d_model,
    )
    int4 = RM.intent_latency_breakdown
    int4_parallel = calc_vla_inference_latency(
        n_params,
        m_int4,
        s_in,
        d_action,
        pi_fp16,
        b_peak,
        bus_efficiency=eta,
        compute_utilization=u,
        parallel_decode=True,
        n_layers=n_layers,
        hidden_dim=d_model,
    )
    int4_three = calc_vla_inference_latency(
        n_params,
        m_int4,
        s_three_cameras,
        d_action,
        pi_fp16,
        b_peak,
        bus_efficiency=eta,
        compute_utilization=u,
        n_layers=n_layers,
        hidden_dim=d_model,
    )
    t_sweep_fp16 = fp16["t_weight_sweep"]
    f_wall = (1 / t_sweep_fp16).to(hertz)
    flops_linear = (2 * n_params.to(count).magnitude * s_in) * flop
    flops_attn = (2 * n_layers * d_model * s_in**2) * flop
    t_prefill = int4["t_prefill"]
    t_int4 = RM.intent_inference_latency
    f_int4 = int4["f_max"]
    rate = RM.intent_rate
    t_period = (1 / rate).to(millisecond)
    t_period_next = (1 / (rate + 1 * hertz)).to(millisecond)
    t_period_5hz = (1 / (5 * hertz)).to(millisecond)
    measured_gap = abs((t_int4 - t_measured) / t_measured).to("dimensionless").magnitude
    parallel_slack = ((t_period_5hz - int4_parallel["t_total"]) / t_period_5hz).to("dimensionless").magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(m_fp16.to(GB).magnitude - 14.0) < 1e-9, f"FP16 weights drifted: {m_fp16}")
    check(abs(t_sweep_fp16.to(millisecond).magnitude - 98.04) < 5e-3, f"FP16 sweep drifted: {t_sweep_fp16}")
    check(abs(f_wall.magnitude - 10.20) < 5e-3, f"Memory-wall rate drifted: {f_wall}")
    check(s_in == 288 and d_action == 7, f"Intent tokens drifted: {s_in}, {d_action}")
    check(intensity_prefill > ridge, "Prefill intensity must exceed the ridge (compute-bound)")
    check(fp16["prefill_bound"] == "compute" and int4["prefill_bound"] == "compute", "Prefill must be compute-bound")
    check(abs(t_prefill.to(millisecond).magnitude - 188.55) < 5e-3, f"Prefill drifted: {t_prefill}")
    check(int4["t_prefill"] == fp16["t_prefill"], "Weight-only quantization must not change the prefill")
    check(abs(fp16["t_total"].to(millisecond).magnitude - 776.78) < 5e-3, f"FP16 total drifted: {fp16['t_total']}")
    check(abs(t_int4.to(millisecond).magnitude - 335.61) < 5e-3, f"INT4 total drifted: {t_int4}")
    check(measured_gap < 0.05, f"Model must stay near the measured INT4 latency: {measured_gap}")
    check(abs(rate.to(hertz).magnitude - 2.0) < 1e-9, f"Intent rate drifted: {rate}")
    check(t_period >= t_int4 > t_period_next, "Rate must be the largest whole-hertz rate the latency supports")
    check(t_int4 > t_period_5hz, "A 5 Hz intent rate must be infeasible at the deployed configuration")
    check(0 < parallel_slack < 0.05, f"Parallel decoding must fit 5 Hz only with thin slack: {parallel_slack}")
    check(abs(int4_three["t_total"].to(millisecond).magnitude - 675.8) < 0.05, f"Three-camera case drifted: {int4_three['t_total']}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    params_str = fmt_params(n_params, precision=0)
    n_layers_str = fmt_int(n_layers)
    d_model_str = fmt_int(d_model, commas=False)
    d_action_str = fmt_int(d_action)
    decode_steps_str = fmt_int(int4["decode_steps"])
    s_in_str = fmt_int(s_in)
    patches_str = fmt_int(patches)
    prompt_tokens_str = fmt_int(s_in - patches)
    u_display = f"{u:g}"
    pi_str = fmt_qty(pi_fp16, unit="TFLOPs/s", precision=0)
    u_pct_str = fmt_percent(u, precision=0, style="prose")
    b_peak_str = fmt_bandwidth(b_peak, unit=GB / second, precision=0)
    eta_pct_str = fmt_percent(eta, precision=0, style="prose")
    b_sus_str = fmt_bandwidth(b_sus, unit=GB / second, precision=1)
    m_fp16_str = fmt_memory(m_fp16, unit=GB, precision=0)
    m_int4_str = fmt_memory(m_int4, unit=GB, precision=1)
    ridge_str = fmt_arithmetic_intensity(ridge, precision=1)
    intensity_str = fmt_arithmetic_intensity(intensity_prefill, precision=0)
    sweep_fp16_str = fmt_latency(t_sweep_fp16, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    sweep_int4_str = fmt_latency(int4["t_weight_sweep"], unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    f_wall_str = fmt_frequency(f_wall, unit=hertz, precision=1)
    prefill_ms_str = fmt_latency(t_prefill, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    prefill_whole_str = fmt_latency(round(t_prefill.to(millisecond).magnitude) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    decode_fp16_str = fmt_latency(round(fp16["t_decode"].to(millisecond).magnitude) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    decode_int4_str = fmt_latency(round(int4["t_decode"].to(millisecond).magnitude) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    total_fp16_str = fmt_latency(round(fp16["t_total"].to(millisecond).magnitude) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    f_fp16_str = fmt_frequency(fp16["f_max"], unit=hertz, precision=1)
    total_int4_str = fmt_latency(round(t_int4.to(millisecond).magnitude) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    f_int4_str = fmt_frequency(f_int4, unit=hertz, precision=2)
    t_measured_str = fmt_latency(t_measured, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    measured_gap_str = fmt_percent(measured_gap, precision=1, style="prose")
    rate_str = fmt_frequency(rate, unit=hertz, precision=0)
    rate_next_str = fmt_frequency(rate + 1 * hertz, unit=hertz, precision=0)
    period_str = fmt_latency(t_period, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    period_next_str = fmt_latency(round(t_period_next.to(millisecond).magnitude) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    period_5hz_str = fmt_latency(t_period_5hz, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    parallel_tokens_str = fmt_int(int4_parallel["prefill_tokens"])
    parallel_total_str = fmt_latency(round(int4_parallel["t_total"].to(millisecond).magnitude) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    parallel_slack_str = fmt_percent(parallel_slack, precision=1, style="prose")
    s_three_str = fmt_int(s_three_cameras)
    three_total_str = fmt_latency(round(int4_three["t_total"].to(millisecond).magnitude) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=0)

    sweep_display_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"t_{{\text{{sweep}}}} = \frac{{M_{{\text{{weights}}}}}}{{B_{{\text{{sustained}}}}}} = \frac{{{m_fp16_str}}}{{{b_sus_str}}} \approx {sweep_fp16_str}, \qquad f \le \frac{{1}}{{t_{{\text{{sweep}}}}}} \approx {f_wall_str}"
    )
    flops_display_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"F_{{\text{{prefill}}}} \approx 2 N S + 2 L d S^2 = {sci_latex(flops_linear, precision=2)} + {sci_latex(flops_attn, precision=2)} \approx {sci_latex(int4['prefill_flops'], precision=2)}\ \text{{FLOP}}"
    )
    prefill_display_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"t_{{\text{{prefill}}}} = \frac{{F_{{\text{{prefill}}}}}}{{u\,\Pi_{{\text{{peak}}}}}} = \frac{{{sci_latex(int4['prefill_flops'], precision=2)}\ \text{{FLOP}}}}{{{u_display} \times {pi_str}}} \approx {prefill_ms_str}"
    )
    fp16_total_display_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"t_{{\text{{FP16}}}} = t_{{\text{{prefill}}}} + (D-1)\,t_{{\text{{sweep}}}} \approx {prefill_whole_str} + {decode_steps_str} \times {sweep_fp16_str} \approx {prefill_whole_str} + {decode_fp16_str} = {total_fp16_str}"
    )
    int4_total_display_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"t_{{\text{{INT4}}}} \approx {prefill_whole_str} + {decode_steps_str} \times {sweep_int4_str} \approx {prefill_whole_str} + {decode_int4_str} = {total_int4_str}, \qquad f \le {f_int4_str}"
    )
```

::: {#fig-patterson-roofline fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Illustrative embodied roofline**: Arithmetic intensity against attainable throughput using the application processor's dense FP16 GPU ceiling and rounded peak memory bandwidth. Single-token weight streaming sits deep in the memory-bound region, while the intent model's prefill, which reuses each fetched weight across all of its input tokens, lies past the ridge where compute binds. Chunk length alone does not determine arithmetic intensity; chunked workloads require measured operations and memory traffic. A separate real-time loop executes accepted waypoints between fresh model updates." fig-alt="Illustrative roofline diagram plotting arithmetic intensity against attainable throughput, with a single-token weight-streaming point on the sloped memory-bound roof, an intent-model prefill point on the flat compute-bound roof, and a ridge separating the two bounds."}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ EMBODIED ROOFLINE (FIGURE)
# │ Context: @fig-patterson-roofline, placed ahead of the memory-wall bound
# │          f <= B_mem / M_weights that it illustrates
# │ Goal:    show single-token decode inside the memory-bound regime and the
# │          intent model's prefill past the ridge
# │ Show:    arithmetic intensity against attainable throughput for an edge part
# │ How:     roof from the registry node; one point represents an FP16
# │          matrix-vector weight sweep, excluding other memory traffic; the
# │          other the intent model's prefill (intensity ~ S, from
# │          calc-brain-intent-model-latency, which therefore runs first)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import viz
from mlsysim import Embodied
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_qty, fmt_arithmetic_intensity, fmt_percent, fmt_display_math, check
from mlsysim.core.units import flop, byte

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

# ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────────────
soc = RM.brain_soc  # category: datasheet; the mobile manipulator's application processor
# Select dense FP16 GPU throughput; the aggregate sparse INT8 rating is incompatible.
node = soc.model_copy(update={"compute": soc.compute.model_copy(update={"peak_flops": soc.compute.precision_flops["fp16"]})})
I_TOKEN = 1.0  # category: illustrative; FLOP/byte for a single-token weight sweep

# ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
peak = node.compute.peak_flops.to("TFLOPs/s").magnitude
bw = node.memory.bandwidth.to("GB/s").magnitude
ridge = peak / (bw / 1000)  # FLOP/byte
attainable = lambda ai: min(bw * ai / 1000, peak)

# ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# 2026-09-28: prevent aggregate sparse INT8 TOPS from entering an FP16 roofline.
check(peak == 43, f"Unexpected dense FP16 roof: {peak}")
check(node.compute.peak_flops < soc.compute.peak_flops, "FP16 roof must not use aggregate INT8 TOPS")
check(abs(ridge - 210.7843) < 0.001, f"Unexpected dense FP16 ridge: {ridge}")

# ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
roof_peak_str = fmt_qty(node.compute.peak_flops, unit="TFLOPs/s", precision=0)
roof_bw_str = fmt_qty(node.memory.bandwidth, unit="GB/s", precision=0)
roof_tdp_str = fmt_qty(soc.tdp_max, unit="W", precision=0)  # datasheet: power mode the roofs assume
roof_tdp_min_str = fmt_qty(soc.tdp_min, unit="W", precision=0)  # datasheet: lowest power mode
roof_ridge_str = fmt_arithmetic_intensity(ridge * flop / byte, precision=1)
roof_attainable_str = fmt_qty(attainable(I_TOKEN) * node.compute.peak_flops.units, unit="TFLOPs/s", precision=3)
roof_fraction_str = fmt_percent(attainable(I_TOKEN) / peak, precision=2, style="prose")
roof_ridge_display_math = fmt_display_math(
    rf"I_{{\text{{ridge}}}} = \frac{{\Pi_{{\text{{peak}}}}}}{{\beta_{{\text{{mem}}}}}} = \frac{{{roof_peak_str}}}{{{roof_bw_str}}} \approx {roof_ridge_str}"
)

points = [
    ("Autoregressive VLA\n(single token)", I_TOKEN),
    (f"Intent-model prefill\n(S = {IntentModelLatency.s_in} tokens)", IntentModelLatency.intensity_prefill.to(flop / byte).magnitude),
]

# ┌── 5. PLOT ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
fig, ax = viz.plot_roofline(node)
COLORS = viz.COLORS
ax.set_ylim(peak * 0.0004, peak * 2)  # keep the single-token point on scale
# Vol IV roles: the ridge is a structural fact, not a hazard, so it is drawn in
# ink rather than red; the two proposer workloads use the proposal role (bronze).
INK, PROPOSAL = "#1A202C", "#B87333"
for ln in ax.lines:
    if ln.get_marker() == "D":
        ln.set_color(INK)
    elif ln.get_linestyle() == ":":
        ln.set_color("#4A5568")
for t in ax.texts:
    s = t.get_text()
    if s.startswith("Ridge Point"):
        # move the ridge label into the empty space above the sloped roof,
        # clear of the prefill point that sits just past the ridge
        t.set_color(INK)
        t.xyann = (ridge * 0.12, peak * 0.55)
        t.arrow_patch.set_color(INK)
    elif s.startswith("MEMORY"):
        t.set_position((t.get_position()[0], peak * 0.008))  # below the roof line, clear of the ridge annotation
for idx, (label, ai) in enumerate(points):
    y = attainable(ai)
    ax.plot(ai, y, "o", ms=8, color=PROPOSAL, zorder=11)
    # the lowest point has no room beneath the roof, so its label goes above
    if idx == 0:
        pos, ha, va = (ai * 0.30, y * 4.0), "left", "bottom"
    else:
        # the prefill point sits just past the ridge; its label drops into the compute-bound region
        pos, ha, va = (ai * 2.5, y * 0.25), "left", "top"
    ax.annotate(
        label,
        xy=(ai, y),
        xytext=pos,
        fontsize=8,
        color=PROPOSAL,
        ha=ha,
        va=va,
        zorder=11,
        arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=PROPOSAL, lw=0.9),  # leader in the label's proposal role
    )

# the reuse a workload would need before it left the memory-bound regime
ax.annotate(
    f"intensity must reach {ridge:.0f} FLOP/byte\nbefore compute binds",
    xy=(ridge, peak * 0.006),
    xytext=(ridge * 0.30, peak * 0.0012),
    fontsize=8,
    color=COLORS["primary"],
    ha="right",
    zorder=11,
    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=COLORS["primary"], lw=0.9),
)
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

:::

To understand the physical consequence of this bandwidth ceiling, consider what happens if a robot attempts to generate continuous motor actions one discrete step at a time through an autoregressive foundation model (such as a multi-billion-parameter VLA model). For a decoder that revisits nonresident weights at each token step, each evaluation streams those weights across the external DRAM bus. In single-token decoding with FP16 weights and request batch size $B = 1$, the dense weight projections become matrix-vector operations ($\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{W}\mathbf{x}$), yielding an arithmetic intensity, the operations performed per byte transferred, of just $I \approx 1.0\,\text{FLOP/byte}$. The sustained memory bandwidth $B_{\text{mem}}$ and model weight footprint $M_{\text{weights}}$ strictly bound the maximum fresh-evaluation frequency:
$$f \le \frac{B_{\text{mem}}}{M_{\text{weights}}}$$
This bound must use the bandwidth actually available to the policy and the weights it transfers at the selected precision. It prices only the weight transfer. A fresh evaluation first reads its input tokens (image patches and the instruction) through the backbone in one pass, the **prefill**\index{Prefill!compute-bound phase}, and that pass reuses every fetched weight across all of those tokens, so arithmetic rather than bandwidth can bind it. The worked example in \ref{nbk-brain-intent-model-latency} prices both terms for the mobile manipulator's intent model. When a decoder emits one token per action dimension, each action dimension requires another token; if each token revisits off-chip parameters, that decode latency scales linearly with degrees of freedom.

This memory wall[^fn-hw-dram-bandwidth] places single-token streaming deep in the memory-bound region of the roofline (@fig-patterson-roofline) [@williams2009roofline]. On the mobile manipulator's application processor it caps the intent model's fresh-evaluation rate, before any vision or decoding work, far below the $100\text{--}1000\,\text{Hz}$ at which stabilization, joint impedance control, and reflex-level collision avoidance run (\ref{nbk-brain-intent-model-latency}). A model renewed that slowly can say where the arm should go, but it cannot close the loop on moving mass, so it proposes waypoints and a faster loop below it tracks them. That conclusion is about timing only. The separate requirement that learned outputs remain proposals, even when they arrive in time, comes from the failures of @sec-brain-cognitive-vulnerabilities.

[Single-token decoding at batch size 1]{.heading-3-inline}
Servers can combine independent requests so that a weight matrix multiplies several input vectors at once, reusing fetched weights. A robot waiting for its next action token often has only one such request. Waiting for future observations to form a batch would add delay, and sequentially dependent action tokens cannot all be evaluated at once by an autoregressive decoder. This limits reuse in those projections. It does not make every operation in an embodied model a matrix-vector product. Image patches, multiple camera views, prompt tokens, and parallel action decoders can expose matrix-matrix work within one robot's request. The low-intensity estimate therefore describes the single-token weight sweep, not the complete perception-and-action workload.

[^fn-hw-dram-bandwidth]: **Autoregressive DRAM Bandwidth Saturation**\index{GPU!memory bandwidth wall}: Sequential action tokens can trigger repeated full-model weight traffic when weights are nonresident and the decoder revisits the backbone; cache behavior and hardware determine the actual bandwidth ceiling. Action chunking is one way to reduce the number of full policy evaluations per unit of physical time.

Repeated off-chip transfers also consume memory-system energy. Their power cost depends on the DRAM, controller, access pattern, and transfer rate, so a bandwidth calculation alone does not establish battery drain or actuator heating. The processor's measured power and the chassis thermal path belong in the shared thermal budget of @sec-body-thermal-duty-cycles.

The roofline model in @fig-patterson-roofline formalizes the hardware boundary governing embodied inference by plotting attainable computational throughput against **arithmetic intensity** ($I$), defined as:
$$I = \frac{\text{FLOPs}}{\text{Bytes transferred from off-chip memory}}$$
Consider the dense weight projections in single-token autoregressive decoding at batch size 1, each evaluating a matrix-vector product $\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{W}\mathbf{x}$. Counting weight traffic alone, with each weight fetched once for that projection, gives an optimistic intensity estimate; activation and context traffic add further bytes. In 16-bit floating-point precision (FP16, 2 bytes per parameter), each weight participates in exactly one multiply-accumulate operation (2 FLOPs), yielding an arithmetic intensity of:
$$I_{\text{token}} = \frac{2\,\text{FLOPs}}{2\,\text{Bytes}} = 1.0\,\text{FLOP/byte}$$
For the mobile manipulator's Jetson AGX Orin application processor in its `{python} roof_tdp_str` maximum-performance power mode, the dense FP16 GPU Tensor Core ceiling is `{python} roof_peak_str`; the aggregate sparse INT8 rating cannot be used for this FP16 workload. Using the model's rounded peak memory bandwidth of `{python} roof_bw_str`, the hardware ridge point occurs at:
`{python} roof_ridge_display_math`
For this weight-streaming example, $I_{\text{token}} = 1.0\,\text{FLOP/byte}$ is far below `{python} roof_ridge_str`, so memory bandwidth sets the roofline ceiling. Attainable throughput is bounded by $\beta_{\text{mem}} \cdot I_{\text{token}}$, or `{python} roof_attainable_str`, about `{python} roof_fraction_str` of the dense FP16 peak. That ratio is a workload throughput bound, not a measurement of how many cores are idle. Both roofs also assume the maximum-performance mode. A battery-powered base often runs a lower power mode, down to `{python} roof_tdp_min_str` on this module, where lower clocks drop both the compute and the bandwidth roof; @sec-body-thermal-duty-cycles sets the mode the machine can sustain.

A fresh evaluation is not a single point on this plot. Its prefill reuses each fetched weight across all of its input tokens and lands past the ridge, while its decode returns to the memory-bound point, one full weight sweep per token. \ref{nbk-brain-intent-model-latency} prices both phases for the machine's intent model.

::: {#nbk-brain-intent-model-latency .callout-notebook title="Pricing one intent-model evaluation"}

**Problem**: The mobile manipulator's intent model is a `{python} IntentModelLatency.params_str`-parameter vision-language model sized after OpenVLA [@kim2024openvla], running on the application processor. Where OpenVLA decodes a step of end-effector motion, the machine's model decodes the same number of tokens to name a target pose (@sec-brain-proposer-interface). How long does one fresh evaluation take, which resource binds each part of it, and what renewal rate can the machine therefore state?

**Variables**:

* Parameters $N =$ `{python} IntentModelLatency.params_str` in $L =$ `{python} IntentModelLatency.n_layers_str` layers of width $d =$ `{python} IntentModelLatency.d_model_str` (Datasheet). The decoder emits $D =$ `{python} IntentModelLatency.d_action_str` tokens, one per output dimension, one after another (Datasheet).
* Input tokens $S =$ `{python} IntentModelLatency.s_in_str`: `{python} IntentModelLatency.patches_str` patches from one $224 \times 224$ view (Derived) plus `{python} IntentModelLatency.prompt_tokens_str` instruction tokens (Illustrative).
* Dense FP16 peak $\Pi_{\text{peak}} =$ `{python} IntentModelLatency.pi_str` (Datasheet), of which the prefill achieves $u =$ `{python} IntentModelLatency.u_pct_str` (Illustrative).
* Peak bandwidth `{python} IntentModelLatency.b_peak_str` (Datasheet), of which `{python} IntentModelLatency.eta_pct_str` is sustained (Illustrative), so $B_{\text{sustained}} =$ `{python} IntentModelLatency.b_sus_str`.
* Stored weights: FP16 (2 bytes per parameter) or INT4 (half a byte), with activations kept in 16 bits (Chosen).

**Math**:

*The memory wall.* FP16 weights occupy `{python} IntentModelLatency.m_fp16_str`. If every evaluation streams them once, the bound above gives
`{python} IntentModelLatency.sweep_display_math`

*The prefill binds on arithmetic.* All $S$ input tokens pass through the backbone together, costing two FLOPs per parameter per token (each weight multiplies one input value and adds the product to a running sum) plus a small attention term:
`{python} IntentModelLatency.flops_display_math`
Each fetched weight now serves $S$ tokens, so the intensity is about $S \approx$ `{python} IntentModelLatency.intensity_str`, beyond the `{python} IntentModelLatency.ridge_str` ridge of @fig-patterson-roofline. Arithmetic binds, and the weight sweep runs underneath it:
`{python} IntentModelLatency.prefill_display_math`

*The decode binds on bandwidth.* The prefill emits the first action token. Each of the remaining $D - 1 =$ `{python} IntentModelLatency.decode_steps_str` tokens is a matrix-vector pass that rereads every weight:
`{python} IntentModelLatency.fp16_total_display_math`
That is about `{python} IntentModelLatency.f_fp16_str`.

*INT4 weights shrink only the bandwidth term.* Storing the weights in four bits cuts them to `{python} IntentModelLatency.m_int4_str` and each sweep to `{python} IntentModelLatency.sweep_int4_str`, but the prefill still multiplies 16-bit activations at the FP16 rate:
`{python} IntentModelLatency.int4_total_display_math`
