*Sensitivity.* Parallel decoding [@kim2025openvlaoft] moves the action tokens into the prefill ($S + D =$ `{python} IntentModelLatency.parallel_tokens_str`) and removes the decode sweeps, giving `{python} IntentModelLatency.parallel_total_str`, only `{python} IntentModelLatency.parallel_slack_str` inside a `{python} IntentModelLatency.period_5hz_str` period with the processor busy for all of it. Three camera views ($S \approx$ `{python} IntentModelLatency.s_three_str`) raise the INT4 total to `{python} IntentModelLatency.three_total_str`.

**Result**: At INT4 one evaluation takes about `{python} IntentModelLatency.total_int4_str`. A published measurement of the same model and quantization on this processor reports `{python} IntentModelLatency.t_measured_str` per frame [@franklin2024openvla], a gap of `{python} IntentModelLatency.measured_gap_str`. That agreement is closer than two illustrative factors deserve. It shows that the model has the right terms, not that $u$ and the sustained fraction are exactly right. A `{python} IntentModelLatency.rate_next_str` rate would need a `{python} IntentModelLatency.period_next_str` period, so the machine runs its intent model at `{python} IntentModelLatency.rate_str`, one evaluation per `{python} IntentModelLatency.period_str`.

**Systems insight**: The binding resource depends on the phase. Prefill reuses weights across tokens and is compute-bound; decode rereads them per token and is bandwidth-bound [@pope2023efficiently]. Weight-only quantization attacks only the second, so after INT4 the compute-bound prefill is most of the latency, and the next gain must come from fewer input tokens, lower-precision arithmetic that the processor's kernels support, or a faster compute roof. @Sec-brain-quantization develops that choice and its accuracy cost.

:::

### Quantizing the intent model {#sec-brain-quantization}

```{python}
#| label: calc-brain-quantization
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ WEIGHT-ONLY QUANTIZATION OF THE INTENT MODEL
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-brain-quantization and @tbl-03-intent-quantization
# │ Goal:    price the intent model at FP16, 8-bit, and INT4 weights against
# │          the published measurements on the same module, and show the
# │          prefill ceiling no weight-only format can pass
# │ Show:    777 / 483 / 336 ms computed vs 840 / 471 / 336 ms measured;
# │          prefill 56 percent of INT4 latency; 5.3 Hz weight-only ceiling;
# │          3.1 percent scale overhead at g = 128
# │ How:     calc_vla_inference_latency at each bytes-per-parameter
# │          (weight-only: prefill unchanged); f_ceiling = 1 / t_prefill
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_memory, fmt_latency, fmt_frequency, fmt_percent, fmt_int, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

def _q_latency(bytes_per_param):
    """Prefill-plus-decode latency of the intent model at one weight precision."""
    L = IntentModelLatency
    return calc_vla_inference_latency(
        L.n_params,
        memory_from_params(L.n_params, bytes_per_param),
        L.s_in,
        L.d_action,
        L.pi_fp16,
        L.b_peak,
        bus_efficiency=L.eta,
        compute_utilization=L.u,
        n_layers=L.n_layers,
        hidden_dim=L.d_model,
    )

class IntentQuantization:
    """The intent model at three weight precisions, computed against measured."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    n_params = IntentModelLatency.n_params  # category: datasheet
    bpp_fp16 = 2.0 * (byte / param)  # category: chosen
    bpp_int8 = 1.0 * (byte / param)  # category: chosen (8-bit weights, 16-bit arithmetic)
    bpp_int4 = RM.intent_weight_bytes_per_param  # category: chosen (deployed)
    # Jetson AI Lab, OpenVLA-7B on AGX Orin 64GB, JetPack 6 (prov:jetson-ai-lab-openvla-orin):
    # mean per-frame latency and action-prediction accuracy on BridgeData V2 episodes that
    # were part of OpenVLA's training data (re-verified 2026-09-29). The page labels the
    # 8-bit row "FP8", but its command runs MLC's q8f16_ft mode: 8-bit weights, FP16 compute.
    meas_fp16 = 840 * millisecond  # category: measured (Hugging Face runtime)
    meas_int8 = 471 * millisecond  # category: measured (q8f16_ft, MLC runtime)
    meas_int4 = RM.intent_reference_latency  # category: measured
    acc_fp16, acc_int8, acc_int4 = 0.953, 0.952, 0.901  # category: measured
    # Kim et al. 2024 (OpenVLA), Table 2: real-robot task success on a desktop GPU
    ovla_bf16, ovla_int8, ovla_int4 = 0.713, 0.581, 0.719  # category: literature
    # Kim et al. 2024, Sec. 5.3: int8 ran at 1.2 Hz on the A5000 evaluation GPU, against
    # the 5 Hz control rate of the training data; the authors attribute the drop to that
    ovla_int8_rate, ovla_train_rate = 1.2 * hertz, 5 * hertz  # category: literature
    group = 128  # category: literature (AWQ group size, Lin et al. 2024, Sec. 5.1)
    scale_bits = 16  # category: chosen (one FP16 scale per group)
    weight_bits = 4  # category: chosen (INT4)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    r_fp16, r_int8, r_int4 = _q_latency(bpp_fp16), _q_latency(bpp_int8), _q_latency(bpp_int4)
    mem_fp16 = memory_from_params(n_params, bpp_fp16).to(GB)
    mem_int8 = memory_from_params(n_params, bpp_int8).to(GB)
    mem_int4 = memory_from_params(n_params, bpp_int4).to(GB)
    gap_fp16 = ((r_fp16["t_total"] - meas_fp16) / meas_fp16).to("dimensionless").magnitude
    gap_int8 = ((r_int8["t_total"] - meas_int8) / meas_int8).to("dimensionless").magnitude
    gap_int4 = ((r_int4["t_total"] - meas_int4) / meas_int4).to("dimensionless").magnitude
    t_prefill = r_int4["t_prefill"]
    prefill_share = (t_prefill / r_int4["t_total"]).to("dimensionless").magnitude
    f_ceiling = (1 / t_prefill).to(hertz)
    scale_overhead = (scale_bits / group) / weight_bits

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(r_fp16["t_prefill"] == r_int8["t_prefill"] == t_prefill, "Weight-only formats must share one prefill")
    check(abs(r_int8["t_total"].to(millisecond).magnitude - 482.66) < 0.01, f"8-bit total drifted: {r_int8['t_total']}")
    check(abs((r_int4["t_total"] - IntentModelLatency.t_int4).to(millisecond).magnitude) < 1e-6, "INT4 row must match the notebook")
    check(abs(gap_int8) < 0.03 and abs(gap_int4) < 0.01, f"Computed must track measured: {gap_int8}, {gap_int4}")
    check(-0.09 < gap_fp16 < -0.06, f"FP16 underestimate drifted: {gap_fp16}")
    check(0.55 < prefill_share < 0.57, f"Prefill share drifted: {prefill_share}")
    check(5.0 < f_ceiling.magnitude < 5.4, f"Weight-only ceiling drifted: {f_ceiling}")
    check(f_ceiling > RM.intent_rate, "The deployed rate must sit below the weight-only ceiling")
    check(abs(scale_overhead - 0.03125) < 1e-12, f"Scale overhead drifted: {scale_overhead}")
    check(ovla_int8_rate < ovla_train_rate, "The int8 run must be slower than the training control rate")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    bpp_fp16_str = fmt_int(bpp_fp16.magnitude)
    bpp_int8_str = fmt_int(bpp_int8.magnitude)
    bpp_int4_str = fmt(bpp_int4.magnitude, precision=1)
    mem_fp16_str = fmt_memory(mem_fp16, unit=GB, precision=0)
    mem_int8_str = fmt_memory(mem_int8, unit=GB, precision=0)
    mem_int4_str = fmt_memory(mem_int4, unit=GB, precision=1)
    sweep_fp16_str = fmt_latency(r_fp16["t_weight_sweep"], unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    sweep_int8_str = fmt_latency(r_int8["t_weight_sweep"], unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    sweep_int4_str = fmt_latency(r_int4["t_weight_sweep"], unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    pred_fp16_str = fmt_latency(round(r_fp16["t_total"].to(millisecond).magnitude) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    pred_int8_str = fmt_latency(round(r_int8["t_total"].to(millisecond).magnitude) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    pred_int4_str = fmt_latency(round(r_int4["t_total"].to(millisecond).magnitude) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    meas_fp16_str = fmt_latency(round(meas_fp16.to(millisecond).magnitude) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    meas_int8_str = fmt_latency(round(meas_int8.to(millisecond).magnitude) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    meas_int4_str = fmt_latency(round(meas_int4.to(millisecond).magnitude) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    acc_fp16_str = fmt_percent(acc_fp16, precision=1, style="symbol")
    acc_int8_str = fmt_percent(acc_int8, precision=1, style="symbol")
    acc_int4_str = fmt_percent(acc_int4, precision=1, style="symbol")
    acc_fp16_prose_str = fmt_percent(acc_fp16, precision=1, style="prose")
    acc_int4_prose_str = fmt_percent(acc_int4, precision=1, style="prose")
    gap_16_str = fmt_percent(abs(gap_fp16), precision=1, style="prose")
    gap_8_str = fmt_percent(abs(gap_int8), precision=1, style="prose")
    gap_4_str = fmt_percent(abs(gap_int4), precision=1, style="prose")
    prefill_share_str = fmt_percent(round(prefill_share, 2), precision=0, style="prose")
    f_ceiling_str = fmt_frequency(f_ceiling, unit=hertz, precision=1)
    group_str = fmt_int(group)
    scale_overhead_pct_str = fmt_percent(scale_overhead, precision=1, style="prose")
    ovla_bf16_str = fmt_percent(ovla_bf16, precision=1, style="prose")
    ovla_int8_str = fmt_percent(ovla_int8, precision=1, style="prose")
    ovla_int4_str = fmt_percent(ovla_int4, precision=1, style="prose")
    ovla_int8_rate_str = fmt_frequency(ovla_int8_rate, unit=hertz, precision=1)
    ovla_train_rate_str = fmt_frequency(ovla_train_rate, unit=hertz, precision=0)
```

The memory wall leaves two levers on the weight term, fewer weights or fewer bytes per weight. A smaller model gives up the recognition the intent model exists to supply, so the machine keeps the `{python} IntentModelLatency.params_str`-parameter model and pulls the second lever. **Quantization**\index{Quantization!weight-only} stores each weight as a low-precision integer plus a shared scale, and reconstructs an approximate weight when the kernel needs it. In the common symmetric form, the weights are divided into groups of $g$, each group keeps one 16-bit scale $s$, and each weight $w_i$ becomes a $b$-bit integer $q_i$ [@jacob2018quantization; @lin2024awq]:
$$s = \frac{\max_{i \in \text{group}} |w_i|}{2^{b-1} - 1}, \qquad q_i = \operatorname{clamp}\!\left(\operatorname{round}\!\left(\frac{w_i}{s}\right),\, -2^{b-1},\, 2^{b-1} - 1\right), \qquad \hat{w}_i = s\, q_i$$
Rounding moves each reconstructed weight $\hat{w}_i$ at most $s/2$ from $w_i$, so one large weight in a group coarsens the step for all the others; choosing which weights to protect from that error is where quantization methods differ. The stored size is $b/8$ bytes per weight plus the scales' share. At $b = 4$ with the `{python} IntentQuantization.group_str`-weight groups that AWQ uses, the scales add `{python} IntentQuantization.scale_overhead_pct_str` to the four-bit payload, which the half-byte-per-parameter figure used here leaves out.

Two families of quantization act on different terms of the latency. *Weight-only* quantization, the machine's choice, restores each weight to 16 bits inside the kernel just before the multiply. It shrinks the bytes every decode sweep rereads, but the arithmetic still runs at the 16-bit rate, so the compute-bound prefill does not move. *Weight-and-activation* quantization makes both operands integers, so the multiplications themselves run on integer units and can shorten the prefill as well. It pays off only when three conditions hold: the processor has fast integer units for that precision, the runtime has kernels for the model's layer shapes, and the activations tolerate the coarser grid. A format without a kernel is only a smaller file.

@Tbl-03-intent-quantization prices the intent model at three weight precisions with the prefill-plus-decode model of \ref{nbk-brain-intent-model-latency}, beside measurements of the same model on the same module [@franklin2024openvla].

| Weight format   |                        Bytes per parameter |                                    Weights |                                 Weight sweep |                            Computed latency |                            Measured latency |                 Action-prediction accuracy |
|:----------------|-------------------------------------------:|-------------------------------------------:|---------------------------------------------:|--------------------------------------------:|--------------------------------------------:|-------------------------------------------:|
| FP16            | `{python} IntentQuantization.bpp_fp16_str` | `{python} IntentQuantization.mem_fp16_str` | `{python} IntentQuantization.sweep_fp16_str` | `{python} IntentQuantization.pred_fp16_str` | `{python} IntentQuantization.meas_fp16_str` | `{python} IntentQuantization.acc_fp16_str` |
| 8-bit           | `{python} IntentQuantization.bpp_int8_str` | `{python} IntentQuantization.mem_int8_str` | `{python} IntentQuantization.sweep_int8_str` | `{python} IntentQuantization.pred_int8_str` | `{python} IntentQuantization.meas_int8_str` | `{python} IntentQuantization.acc_int8_str` |
| INT4 (deployed) | `{python} IntentQuantization.bpp_int4_str` | `{python} IntentQuantization.mem_int4_str` | `{python} IntentQuantization.sweep_int4_str` | `{python} IntentQuantization.pred_int4_str` | `{python} IntentQuantization.meas_int4_str` | `{python} IntentQuantization.acc_int4_str` |

: **Weight-only quantization of the intent model**: Computed latency uses the sustained bandwidth and the illustrative prefill utilization of @sec-brain-memory-wall; measured latency and action-prediction accuracy are the Jetson AI Lab means over BridgeData V2 episodes on the 64 GB Jetson AGX Orin module [@franklin2024openvla]. The episodes were part of the model's training data, so the accuracy column measures how faithfully each format reproduces the FP16 model, not how well it generalizes. The source labels its 8-bit build FP8, but runs it in a mode that stores 8-bit weights and computes in 16 bits, the same weight-only form the computed row assumes. The FP16 measurement used a general-purpose runtime (Hugging Face) rather than the optimized one (MLC) used for the other two. {#tbl-03-intent-quantization tbl-colwidths="[16,12,12,12,16,16,16]"}

The computed and measured columns agree within `{python} IntentQuantization.gap_8_str` for the 8-bit format and `{python} IntentQuantization.gap_4_str` for INT4. The model underestimates the FP16 run by `{python} IntentQuantization.gap_16_str`, consistent with that run's slower runtime, so the comparison supports the model's two terms rather than its exact constants. The table also shows where weight-only quantization stops paying. Each halving of the bytes halves the sweep, but the `{python} IntentModelLatency.prefill_ms_str` prefill is untouched, and at INT4 it is already `{python} IntentQuantization.prefill_share_str` of the latency. Even weights that cost no bytes at all would leave the prefill, so no weight-only format can lift the intent model above `{python} IntentQuantization.f_ceiling_str`. Beyond that ceiling, the gain must come from integer arithmetic in the prefill, fewer input tokens, or a processor with a higher compute roof.

The last column carries the cost. On this module the INT4 build's action-prediction accuracy fell from `{python} IntentQuantization.acc_fp16_prose_str` to `{python} IntentQuantization.acc_int4_prose_str` [@franklin2024openvla]. OpenVLA's authors, measuring task success on a real robot with a desktop GPU, found a different pattern. INT4 weights kept `{python} IntentQuantization.ovla_int4_str` success against `{python} IntentQuantization.ovla_bf16_str` for bfloat16, while INT8 weights through a general-purpose quantization library fell to `{python} IntentQuantization.ovla_int8_str`. The cause was time, not rounding. The library's added quantization operations cost more than the saved bytes, so the INT8 policy ran at `{python} IntentQuantization.ovla_int8_rate_str` on the evaluation GPU, against the `{python} IntentQuantization.ovla_train_rate_str` control rate of its training data, and the robot met each observation later than the demonstrations had [@kim2024openvla]. On the module an 8-bit format was nearly free and INT4 cost accuracy; on the desktop GPU the 8-bit build lost success through its slower loop and INT4 was nearly free. The two 8-bit results used different software and kernels, and the two studies scored different tasks, so the pair shows that a bit width alone does not predict the outcome; the quantization method, the kernels, the control rate they allow, and the task together do. A quantized checkpoint is a different model. It must be evaluated on the machine's own contact tasks at the deployed precision, carry its own calibration, and be named as such by the `model_id` of the proposal payload (@sec-brain-proposer-information). The footprint saving also has a systems value. Dropping from `{python} IntentQuantization.mem_fp16_str` to `{python} IntentQuantization.mem_int4_str` of weights returns memory that retained context and perception also need. How much of the computed saving survives when the cameras and the chunk policy share the bus is a measurement that @sec-placement-resource-contention makes under load.

### Action chunking {#sec-brain-action-chunking}

The memory bound limits how often a large model can revise its proposal. A controller can track previously admitted motion between those revisions, but a policy that supplies only one future setpoint leaves little planned motion available while it computes. Predicting a trajectory segment gives the controller a sequence to track without making the next fresh observation arrive sooner.

```{python}
#| label: calc-brain-chunk-supply-demand
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ BANDWIDTH DEMANDED BY SINGLE-STEP VERSUS CHUNKED SUPPLY
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: the supply-rate paragraph in @sec-brain-action-chunking
# │ Goal:    show why one weight sweep per setpoint cannot feed the arm
# │ Show:    40 Hz x 14 GB = 560 GB/s, 3.9x the 142.8 GB/s sustained; H = 16
# │          cuts demand to 35.0 GB/s, 24.5 percent of sustained (25 ms
# │          setpoint step since M5, 2026-09-28; was 50 Hz / 700 GB/s)
# │ How:     demand = f_supply x M_weights; chunked = demand / H
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_frequency, fmt_bandwidth, fmt_int, fmt_percent, fmt, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

class ChunkSupplyDemand:
    """Weight-sweep bandwidth demanded at the setpoint rate, single-step versus chunked."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    f_supply = (1 / RM.chunk_step).to(hertz)  # category: derived (setpoint rate)
    horizon = RM.chunk_horizon  # category: chosen
    m_fp16 = IntentModelLatency.m_fp16  # category: derived (FP16 intent weights)
    b_sus = IntentModelLatency.b_sus  # category: derived (sustained bandwidth)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    demand = (f_supply * m_fp16).to(GB / second)
    over = (demand / b_sus).to("dimensionless").magnitude
    demand_chunk = (demand / horizon).to(GB / second)
    share_chunk = (demand_chunk / b_sus).to("dimensionless").magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(f_supply.magnitude - 40.0) < 1e-9, f"Setpoint rate drifted: {f_supply}")
    check(abs(demand.magnitude - 560.0) < 1e-6, f"Single-step demand drifted: {demand}")
    check(over > 1, "Single-step supply must exceed the sustained bandwidth")
    check(demand_chunk < b_sus, "Chunked supply must fit the sustained bandwidth")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    f_supply_str = fmt_frequency(f_supply, unit=hertz, precision=0)
    f_supply_num_str = fmt_int(f_supply.magnitude)
    demand_str = fmt_bandwidth(demand, unit=GB / second, precision=0)
    over_str = fmt(over, precision=1)
    horizon_str = fmt_int(horizon)
    demand_chunk_str = fmt_bandwidth(demand_chunk, unit=GB / second, precision=0)
    share_chunk_str = fmt_percent(share_chunk, precision=1, style="prose")
```

```{python}
#| label: calc-brain-chunk-schedule
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE CHUNK POLICY'S RENEWAL SCHEDULE
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: the supply, replanning, and reaction bullets and the temporal
# │          ensembling paragraph in @sec-brain-action-chunking
# │ Goal:    give the three rates of the selected chunk policy and show that
# │          its renewal falls on the setpoint grid
# │ Show:    40 Hz supply (25 ms step); 20 Hz / 50 ms renewal = 2 setpoints;
# │          50 + 40 = 90 ms reaction; 8 chunks cover each step (H = 16)
# │ How:     RM.chunk_schedule (calc_chunk_renewal_schedule), 2026-09-28, M5
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
import math
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_frequency, fmt_latency, fmt_int, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

class ChunkSchedule:
    """Setpoint supply, renewal, and reaction timing of the machine's chunk policy."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    step = RM.chunk_step.to(millisecond)  # category: chosen (setpoint step)
    f_replan = RM.chunk_rate  # category: chosen (renewal rate)
    t_infer = RM.chunk_inference_latency.to(millisecond)  # category: illustrative (P99 incl. vision)
    horizon = RM.chunk_horizon  # category: chosen
    sched = RM.chunk_schedule  # category: derived (calc_chunk_renewal_schedule)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    f_supply = (1 / step).to(hertz)
    t_replan = sched["renewal_period"]
    n_per_renewal = sched["setpoints_per_renewal"]
    t_reaction = sched["open_loop_span"]
    n_overlap = sched["overlapping_chunks"]
    n_frozen = math.ceil((t_infer / step).to("dimensionless").magnitude)  # setpoints that execute during one inference

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(step.magnitude - 25.0) < 1e-9, f"Setpoint step drifted: {step}")
    check(abs(t_replan.magnitude - 50.0) < 1e-9, f"Renewal period drifted: {t_replan}")
    check(n_per_renewal == 2, f"Setpoints per renewal drifted: {n_per_renewal}")
    check(abs(t_reaction.magnitude - 90.0) < 1e-9, f"Reaction latency drifted: {t_reaction}")
    check(n_overlap == 8, f"Overlapping chunks drifted: {n_overlap}")
    check(n_frozen == 2 and n_frozen < horizon, f"Committed prefix drifted: {n_frozen}")
    # margin_action_chunk_windows_strip.svg fig-alt hand-types 16 steps, 2 past, 2 run, 12 buffer.
    check(horizon == 16 and horizon - n_frozen - n_per_renewal == 12, f"Chunk-strip margin labels drifted: H = {horizon}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    f_supply_str = fmt_frequency(f_supply, unit=hertz, precision=0)
    step_str = fmt_latency(step, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    step_us_str = fmt_int(step.to(microsecond).magnitude)
    f_replan_str = fmt_frequency(f_replan, unit=hertz, precision=0)
    t_replan_str = fmt_latency(t_replan, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_infer_str = fmt_latency(t_infer, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_reaction_str = fmt_latency(t_reaction, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    n_per_renewal_str = fmt_int(n_per_renewal)
    n_overlap_str = fmt_int(n_overlap)
    n_frozen_str = fmt_int(n_frozen)
    horizon_str = fmt_int(horizon)
```

[Supply rate vs. closed-loop reaction latency]{.heading-3-inline}
To supply dense waypoints despite slow full-model inference, modern physical AI policies employ **action chunking**\index{Action chunking!temporal trajectory} (\ref{dfn-brain-action-chunking}) [@zhao2023learning; @chi2024diffusionpolicy]. Each chunk then crosses the proposal boundary as one packet, the chunk payload of @sec-nervous-cadences. The transfer saving follows from reusing one evaluation across several outputs.

::: {#dfn-brain-action-chunking .callout-definition title="Temporal action chunking"}

***Temporal action chunking***\index{Temporal action chunking!definition}\index{Action chunking!definition} is the policy formulation that predicts an entire horizon of $H$ future continuous actions $\mathbf{A}_{t:t+H-1} = [\mathbf{a}_t, \dots, \mathbf{a}_{t+H-1}]$ in a single neural evaluation or diffusion rollout, amortizing parameter memory transfers across extended physical execution windows.

1.  **Significance**: On a bandwidth-limited device, repeating a full model evaluation for every action can be too slow for millisecond control. Temporal action chunking can reuse a backbone evaluation across multiple waypoints; it does not make fresh observations or policy decisions arrive at the waypoint rate. A downstream controller tracks the accepted trajectory between model updates.
2.  **Distinction**: Unlike single-step Markovian policies $\mathbf{a}_t \sim \pi(\cdot \mid \mathbf{o}_t)$ that re-evaluate the full neural network at every control step, action chunking deliberately generates multi-step feedforward trajectories, utilizing receding-horizon execution and blending across overlapping chunks to reconcile slow neural deliberation with fast closed-loop control.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Executing action chunks open-loop without continuous temporal smoothing or runtime safety filtering. Without smooth blending across overlapping chunk boundaries, switching between independently generated horizons injects acceleration jumps and torque shocks that excite mechanical gearbox resonances.

:::

Predicting a horizon of $H$ actions per forward pass spreads the multi-gigabyte DRAM weight streaming cost over $H \times \Delta t_{\text{step}}$ seconds of physical execution. On the mobile manipulator's application processor, a `{python} IntentModelLatency.params_str` FP16 model (`{python} IntentModelLatency.m_fp16_str`) generating single-step actions at the `{python} ChunkSupplyDemand.f_supply_str` setpoint rate would demand `{python} ChunkSupplyDemand.f_supply_num_str` $\times$ `{python} IntentModelLatency.m_fp16_str` $=$ `{python} ChunkSupplyDemand.demand_str` of memory bandwidth, `{python} ChunkSupplyDemand.over_str` times the `{python} IntentModelLatency.b_sus_str` it can sustain. A chunk of $H =$ `{python} ChunkSupplyDemand.horizon_str` waypoints cuts that demand to `{python} ChunkSupplyDemand.demand_chunk_str`, `{python} ChunkSupplyDemand.share_chunk_str` of the sustained bandwidth, if one sweep supplies each full chunk. More frequent replanning, decoder work, and competing memory traffic consume additional bandwidth. The saving is in weight traffic per supplied waypoint, not an equal gain in arithmetic intensity; predicting a chunk adds decoder work, and its position on the roofline depends on the operations performed and the bytes actually transferred.

Predicting a sequence also changes how a learned policy uses recent actions, but chunking alone does not establish that the policy attends to the right evidence or recovers from an unfamiliar contact. Those properties depend on training and closed-loop evaluation. The supply calculation establishes only the weight traffic needed for the stated execution schedule.

The selected smaller policy has a separate illustrative schedule. Three quantities distinguish its setpoint supply from the delay before a new observation changes a proposal:

* *Setpoint supply cadence* ($f_{\text{supply}} = 1/\Delta t_{\text{step}} =$ `{python} ChunkSchedule.f_supply_str`, $\Delta t_{\text{step}} =$ `{python} ChunkSchedule.step_str`): The rate at which the trajectory queue delivers discrete waypoints to the joint servo loop.
* *Policy replanning rate* ($f_{\text{replan}} =$ `{python} ChunkSchedule.f_replan_str`, period $T_{\text{replan}} =$ `{python} ChunkSchedule.t_replan_str`): The cadence at which the smaller chunk policy begins an evaluation from fresh sensory frames. The period is chosen as a whole number of setpoint steps, here `{python} ChunkSchedule.n_per_renewal_str`, so that every renewal begins on a setpoint boundary.
* *Closed-loop reaction latency* ($T_{\text{reaction}} = T_{\text{replan}} + t_{\text{infer}} =$ `{python} ChunkSchedule.t_replan_str` $+$ `{python} ChunkSchedule.t_infer_str` $=$ `{python} ChunkSchedule.t_reaction_str`): The worst sampling-phase wait plus the assumed inference time until a revised proposal is available, excluding further admission and physical response delay.

In this illustrative schedule, a disturbance immediately after capture can wait up to `{python} ChunkSchedule.t_reaction_str` for a revised learned proposal, before any additional admission and actuation delay. The independent permission path need not wait for that revision: current qualified evidence can trigger a protective response while the policy computes. Its ability to detect the relevant obstacle and complete a feasible response needs its own timing and sensing evidence. Chunking keeps candidate waypoints available; it establishes neither that response nor its deadline.

```{python}
#| label: calc-brain-decoder-families
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE THREE DECODER FAMILIES PRICED ON THE MACHINE'S PROCESSOR
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: the decoder-family paragraphs in @sec-brain-action-chunking
# │ Goal:    show what one fresh H = 16 chunk costs if the intent-sized
# │          backbone produced it, for each decoder family
# │ Show:    every family pays the ~189 ms compute-bound prefill; binned
# │          autoregressive ~2.9 s, FAST (30 tokens) ~0.9 s, parallel ~0.26 s,
# │          flow expert (300M, 10 steps) ~0.24 s; none fits the 50 ms period
# │ How:     calc_vla_inference_latency (INT4 backbone) with D = H x d_a, the
# │          FAST low-end token count, or parallel decoding; expert steps are
# │          max(compute, (expert weights + prefix KV) / B_sustained)
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_latency, fmt_memory, fmt_int, fmt_multiple, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

def _backbone(action_tokens, parallel=False):
    """The INT4 intent-sized backbone emitting action_tokens (sequential unless parallel)."""
    L = IntentModelLatency
    return calc_vla_inference_latency(
        L.n_params,
        L.m_int4,
        L.s_in,
        action_tokens,
        L.pi_fp16,
        L.b_peak,
        bus_efficiency=L.eta,
        compute_utilization=L.u,
        parallel_decode=parallel,
        n_layers=L.n_layers,
        hidden_dim=L.d_model,
    )

class DecoderFamilies:
    """One fresh H-step chunk from the intent-sized backbone, per decoder family."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    horizon = RM.chunk_horizon  # category: chosen (the machine's H)
    d_a = IntentModelLatency.d_action  # category: datasheet (values per action)
    fast_tokens = StateOfPractice.fast_tok_lo  # category: literature (FAST low end, Pertsch et al. 2025)
    expert_params = StateOfPractice.pi0_expert  # category: literature (pi0 action expert)
    expert_steps = StateOfPractice.pi0_steps  # category: literature (pi0 integration steps)
    expert_bpp = 2 * (byte / param)  # category: chosen (16-bit expert weights)
    kv_per_token = (2 * IntentModelLatency.n_layers * IntentModelLatency.d_model * 2 * byte).to(MB)  # derived; full-width FP16 K and V
    b_sus = IntentModelLatency.b_sus  # category: derived
    pi_eff = IntentModelLatency.u * IntentModelLatency.pi_fp16  # category: derived (achieved FP16 rate)
    t_period = ChunkSchedule.t_replan  # category: derived (the machine's renewal period)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    n_binned = horizon * d_a
    r_binned = _backbone(n_binned)
    r_fast = _backbone(fast_tokens)
    r_parallel = _backbone(n_binned, parallel=True)
    r_prefill = _backbone(1)  # prefill only: the first token comes out of the prefill
    t_prefill = r_prefill["t_total"]
    expert_mem = memory_from_params(expert_params, expert_bpp).to(MB)
    prefix_kv = (kv_per_token * IntentModelLatency.s_in).to(MB)
    t_step_bw = ((expert_mem + prefix_kv) / b_sus).to(millisecond)
    t_step_compute = (2 * expert_params.to(param).magnitude * horizon * flop / pi_eff).to(millisecond)
    t_step = max(t_step_bw, t_step_compute)
    t_expert = (t_prefill + expert_steps * t_step).to(millisecond)
    t_binned, t_fast, t_parallel = r_binned["t_total"], r_fast["t_total"], r_parallel["t_total"]
    spread = (t_binned / t_expert).to("dimensionless").magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(n_binned == 112, f"Binned token count drifted: {n_binned}")
    check(abs((t_prefill - IntentModelLatency.t_prefill).to(millisecond).magnitude) < 1e-6, "Prefill must match the notebook")
    check(t_step_bw > t_step_compute, "Expert steps must be bandwidth-bound on this processor")
    check(t_binned > t_fast > t_parallel > t_expert > t_prefill, "Family ordering drifted")
    check(abs(t_binned.to(millisecond).magnitude - 2909.1) < 0.1, f"Binned total drifted: {t_binned}")
    check(abs(t_expert.to(millisecond).magnitude - 241.14) < 0.01, f"Expert total drifted: {t_expert}")
    check(abs(t_parallel.to(millisecond).magnitude - 264.37) < 0.01, f"Parallel total drifted: {t_parallel}")
    check(t_prefill > t_period, "The backbone prefill alone must exceed the renewal period")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    n_binned_str = fmt_int(n_binned)
    fast_tokens_str = fmt_int(fast_tokens)
    t_prefill_str = fmt_latency(round(t_prefill.to(millisecond).magnitude) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_binned_str = fmt_latency(t_binned.to(second), unit=second, precision=1)
    t_fast_str = fmt_latency(round(t_fast.to(millisecond).magnitude) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_parallel_str = fmt_latency(round(t_parallel.to(millisecond).magnitude) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_expert_str = fmt_latency(round(t_expert.to(millisecond).magnitude) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_step_str = fmt_latency(t_step, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    expert_mem_str = fmt_memory(expert_mem, unit=MB, precision=0)
    prefix_kv_str = fmt_memory(round(prefix_kv.magnitude) * MB, unit=MB, precision=0)
    spread_mult_str = fmt_multiple(round(spread), precision=0)
    t_period_str = fmt_latency(t_period, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
```

[Pricing the decoder families]{.heading-3-inline}
The three decoder families of @sec-brain-learned-representations differ in how they turn one observation into a chunk, and the machine's processor prices that difference. Suppose the intent-sized backbone, with its deployed INT4 weights, produced one fresh chunk of $H =$ `{python} ChunkSchedule.horizon_str` setpoints of `{python} IntentModelLatency.d_action_str` values each. Every family first pays the same compute-bound prefill of the observation, about `{python} DecoderFamilies.t_prefill_str`, and then the families part ways:

* Binned autoregressive tokens need `{python} DecoderFamilies.n_binned_str` sequential decode steps, each rereading the backbone weights, for about `{python} DecoderFamilies.t_binned_str`.
* FAST tokens cut the sequence to about `{python} DecoderFamilies.fast_tokens_str` tokens, the count its authors report per arm for a one-second chunk and therefore generous for this shorter chunk, about `{python} DecoderFamilies.t_fast_str`, still sequential.
* A parallel head folds every action into one longer prefill, about `{python} DecoderFamilies.t_parallel_str`.
* A $\pi_0$-sized action expert of `{python} DecoderFamilies.expert_mem_str` in 16-bit weights integrates `{python} StateOfPractice.pi0_steps_str` steps. Each step rereads the expert and the backbone's `{python} DecoderFamilies.prefix_kv_str` of cached keys and values rather than the backbone weights, about `{python} DecoderFamilies.t_step_str` per step on bandwidth, for about `{python} DecoderFamilies.t_expert_str` in all. @Sec-appendix-ml-diffusion derives the noise-prediction and flow-matching objectives these experts train on.

The decoder choice spans `{python} DecoderFamilies.spread_mult_str` in latency on the same backbone, the cost that parallel decoding and action experts were introduced to remove [@kim2025openvlaoft; @black2024pi0]. None of the four renews within the chunk policy's `{python} DecoderFamilies.t_period_str` period, because the prefill alone exceeds it. A large backbone that reads each observation fresh cannot also be the fast renewer on this processor, whatever its decoder. Deployed dual systems reach the same conclusion by assigning renewal to a separate, smaller model, as @tbl-03-state-of-practice records, and the machine does the same with its ACT chunk policy.

Two further points follow from the expert design. Its weights, hundreds of megabytes, far exceed the processor's on-chip caches, so each refinement step pays another off-chip transfer; a head small enough to stay resident would change that term, and the processor's cache capacity decides whether it can. Reducing the number of refinement steps shortens the decoder, provided the proposals keep the required task quality, but it does not touch the prefill of a fresh observation.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_action_chunk_windows_strip.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Sequence strip of one action chunk of 16 steps at 25 ms each: the first two steps are already past when the chunk arrives, the next two run for 50 ms until the successor chunk takes over, and the remaining 12 are buffer that later chunks overlap."}

*Overlapping action chunks blend predictions across receding temporal execution windows.*
:::

Whatever the decoder, chunking creates one more problem, **chunk seam continuity**. Because each action chunk is generated independently from rolling sensory observations, the tail of chunk $k$ and the head of chunk $k+1$ may exhibit slight positional and velocity discrepancies. If a controller concatenated these chunks directly, the resulting step-discontinuities in acceleration would inject large jerk ($\dddot{\mathbf{q}}$) into the physical linkages, inducing mechanical shock, acoustic vibration, cycloidal pin wear, and motor overcurrent faults.

To reduce discontinuities between overlapping chunks, systems can implement **temporal ensembling**\index{Temporal ensembling!trajectory smoothing}, blending overlapping trajectory predictions via exponentially weighted averaging:

$$\mathbf{a}_t = \frac{\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} w_k \, \mathbf{a}_t^{(k)}}{\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} w_k}, \quad w_k = \exp(-m \cdot k)$$

where $\mathbf{a}_t^{(k)}$ is the action for step $t$ predicted by the $k$-th oldest of the $n$ chunks that cover step $t$ ($k = 0$ is the oldest), and $m > 0$ is a tunable weighting rate. Following ACT, the oldest prediction receives the largest weight, which favors smoothness over responsiveness; a smaller $m$ lets new observations enter the blend faster [@zhao2023learning]. The formula assumes that the policy is queried at every control step, as ACT does, so that $n = \min(t + 1, H)$. The mobile manipulator's chunk policy renews every `{python} ChunkSchedule.n_per_renewal_str` setpoints instead, and because its `{python} ChunkSchedule.t_replan_str` renewal period is a whole number of `{python} ChunkSchedule.step_str` steps, each new chunk starts on a setpoint boundary. The same formula then applies with $k$ counting renewals rather than steps. A `{python} ChunkSchedule.horizon_str`-setpoint chunk renewed every `{python} ChunkSchedule.n_per_renewal_str` setpoints gives at most $n =$ `{python} ChunkSchedule.n_overlap_str` overlapping predictions at any step. A renewal period that fell between setpoints would leave each chunk's first action off the grid, and the blend would first have to interpolate every chunk onto common setpoint times. The permission path interpolates the blended waypoints below the proposal boundary (@sec-nervous-cadences).

Ensembling has two limits. It averages, and the average of two valid predictions need not be valid: if an older chunk passes left of an obstacle and a newer one passes right, the blend steers between them [@black2025realtime]. It also ignores what executes while the policy computes. With the assumed `{python} ChunkSchedule.t_infer_str` inference and `{python} ChunkSchedule.step_str` setpoints, the arm consumes `{python} ChunkSchedule.n_frozen_str` setpoints of the previous chunk before the new one exists, so no new prediction can change them. *Real-time chunking*\index{Real-time chunking!committed prefix} treats those setpoints as committed. It freezes the part of the previous chunk that will execute during inference and has a flow or diffusion policy fill in the rest of the new chunk so that it agrees with that frozen prefix, rather than blending afterward [@black2025realtime]. The method arrives from the learning side at this chapter's distinction, in which the committed prefix is motion already admitted and the tail is a buffer that the next evaluation may still rewrite. @Sec-training-multimodality-breakdown derives why averaging demonstrated routes fails, and @sec-training-action-chunking treats chunk seams from the training side.

::: {.callout-perspective title="The temporal ensembling jerk trap"}
Exponentially weighted temporal ensembling averages overlapping predictions, but averaging sampled setpoints alone guarantees neither continuous position nor continuous velocity between samples or at chunk boundaries. A downstream interpolator determines those properties. If successive chunks disagree in slope, a controller can receive a step in commanded velocity even when position remains continuous. In joint PD tracking ($\boldsymbol{\tau} = \mathbf{K}_p \mathbf{e} + \mathbf{K}_d \dot{\mathbf{e}}$), that velocity jump produces a finite torque step. With derivative gain $K_d = 40\,\text{N}\cdot\text{m}\cdot\text{s/rad}$ and velocity discontinuity $\Delta \dot{q} = 0.5\,\text{rad/s}$, the derivative term changes by $\Delta \tau = K_d \Delta \dot{q} = 20\,\text{N}\cdot\text{m}$. Dividing by the servo period would instead describe a torque slew rate, not a torque. Abrupt torque changes can excite mechanical resonances or exceed drive limits. Interpolation must match position, velocity, and acceleration at adjoining segments to provide $C^2$ continuity, while enforcing the machine's velocity, acceleration, and torque limits. Smoothness alone does not establish that the requested motion is feasible.
:::

A chunked policy therefore has two rates that a single "action rate" conflates: the spacing of the waypoints it supplies and the interval between the fresh observations that change them. Supplying more waypoints from one sensory context does not refresh the observation on which they depend. A downstream controller can use current state measurements while tracking admitted waypoints between renewals, and its feedback corrects tracking errors within its capabilities, but a newly perceived obstacle still requires a timely checking or replanning response. The worked mobile-manipulator budget below keeps the two rates apart, and @fig-03-chunk-supply-horizon draws them on the machine's own clock once the conveyor pick has supplied the evidence horizon.

### Two proposers and the evidence horizon {#sec-brain-two-proposers}

Chunking reduces the cost per waypoint, but the decoder pricing showed that each fresh context still waits for the large backbone's prefill, whatever the decoder. We can now budget the split that follows, a slow intent model above a fast chunk policy, on the warehouse mobile manipulator, and then ask how long each chunk the fast policy supplies stays true. Notebook \ref{nbk-brain-lpddr5-memory-wall-bottleneck-action-chunking} applies the memory bound to the split and checks whether chunking alone could give the larger model the required renewal cadence.

```{python}
#| label: calc-brain-action-chunking-lpddr5
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ MEMORY WALL AND THE MACHINE'S TWO PROPOSERS
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: nbk-brain-lpddr5-memory-wall-bottleneck-action-chunking and the
# │          memory-wall paragraphs that follow it
# │ Goal:    show why the mobile manipulator's intent model cannot renew a
# │          proposal every few tens of milliseconds while its chunk policy can
# │ Show:    98.0 ms per FP16 intent-model weight sweep (about 10 Hz before
# │          vision); 6.1 ms amortized weight-sweep time per setpoint over
# │          H = 16; 1.12 ms per chunk-policy sweep; intent 2 Hz with a computed
# │          336 ms INT4 latency (calc-brain-intent-model-latency); chunk policy
# │          20 Hz / 40 ms
# │ How:     t_stream = M_weights / (B_peak * dram_efficiency);
# │          tau_step = t_stream / H (calc_action_chunk_streaming_amortization)
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import (
    fmt_params,
    fmt_memory,
    fmt_bandwidth,
    fmt_latency,
    fmt_time,
    fmt_frequency,
    fmt_percent,
    fmt_int,
    fmt_display_math,
    check,
)

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

class ActionChunkingLPDDR5:
    """Memory wall and action chunking amortization on the machine's application processor."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    model = RM.intent_model  # category: chosen (the machine's intent model)
    chunk_model = RM.chunk_model  # category: chosen (the machine's chunk policy)
    soc = RM.brain_soc  # category: datasheet (application processor)
    params = model.parameters  # category: datasheet
    chunk_params = chunk_model.parameters  # category: datasheet
    bytes_per_param = 2 * (byte / param)  # category: chosen; FP16 weight storage
    bytes_per_param_int4 = 0.5 * (byte / param)  # category: chosen; INT4 alternative
    b_peak = soc.memory.bandwidth  # category: datasheet
    soc_mem = soc.memory.capacity  # category: datasheet
    bus_efficiency = RM.dram_efficiency  # category: illustrative; sustained fraction of peak
    chunk_horizon = RM.chunk_horizon  # category: chosen
    chunk_step = RM.chunk_step  # category: chosen
    intent_rate = RM.intent_rate  # category: chosen
    intent_latency = RM.intent_inference_latency  # category: derived (calc_vla_inference_latency)
    chunk_rate = RM.chunk_rate  # category: chosen
    chunk_latency = RM.chunk_inference_latency  # category: illustrative; P99 incl. vision
    kv_layers = model.layers  # category: datasheet
    kv_hidden = model.hidden_dim  # category: datasheet
    kv_bytes = 2 * byte  # category: chosen; FP16 key and value storage
    cameras = 3  # category: illustrative; synchronized RGB streams
    patches_per_frame = 256  # category: derived; patch tokens per 224 x 224 frame at P = 14
    context_tokens = 800  # category: illustrative; visual plus language and proprioception tokens per step
    history_window = 5 * second  # category: illustrative; retained visual history
    history_rate = 10 * Hz  # category: illustrative; frames retained per second of history

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    weight_mem = memory_from_params(params, bytes_per_param)
    weight_mem_int4 = memory_from_params(params, bytes_per_param_int4)
    res = calc_action_chunk_streaming_amortization(
        model_weight_memory=weight_mem,
        memory_bandwidth=b_peak,
        chunk_horizon=chunk_horizon,
        bus_efficiency=bus_efficiency,
    )
    b_sustained = res["b_sustained"]
    t_stream = res["t_stream"]
    f_single = res["f_single"]
    tau_step = res["tau_step"]
    chunk_span = (chunk_horizon * chunk_step).to(millisecond)

    chunk_weight_mem = memory_from_params(chunk_params, bytes_per_param)
    chunk_res = calc_action_chunk_streaming_amortization(
        model_weight_memory=chunk_weight_mem,
        memory_bandwidth=b_peak,
        chunk_horizon=chunk_horizon,
        bus_efficiency=bus_efficiency,
    )
    chunk_t_stream = chunk_res["t_stream"]

    visual_tokens = cameras * patches_per_frame
    kv_per_token = (2 * kv_layers * kv_hidden * kv_bytes).to(MB)
    kv_per_frame = (kv_per_token * visual_tokens).to(MB)
    history_frames = round((history_window * history_rate).to("dimensionless").magnitude)
    kv_history_visual = (kv_per_frame * history_frames).to(GB)
    kv_per_step = (kv_per_token * context_tokens).to(MB)
    kv_history = (kv_per_step * history_frames).to(GB)
    combined_mem = (weight_mem + kv_history).to(GB)
    combined_ratio = (combined_mem / soc_mem).to("dimensionless").magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(weight_mem.to(GB).magnitude - 14.0) < 0.1, f"Unexpected weight footprint: {weight_mem}")
    check(abs(b_sustained.to(GB / second).magnitude - 142.80) < 0.05, f"Unexpected sustained bandwidth: {b_sustained}")
    check(abs(t_stream.to(millisecond).magnitude - 98.04) < 0.005, f"Unexpected intent sweep: {t_stream}")
    check(abs(f_single.magnitude - 10.20) < 0.05, f"Unexpected single-sweep frequency: {f_single}")
    check(chunk_horizon == 16, f"Unexpected chunk horizon: {chunk_horizon}")
    check(abs(tau_step.to(millisecond).magnitude - 6.13) < 0.01, f"Unexpected per-setpoint sweep time: {tau_step}")
    check(abs(chunk_span.magnitude - 400.0) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected chunk span: {chunk_span}")  # 16 x 25 ms (M5)
    # 2026-09-28: ACT corrected to about 80M parameters (Zhao et al. 2023); intent
    # latency now computed from prefill plus decode (decision M2).
    check(abs(chunk_t_stream.to(millisecond).magnitude - 1.1204) < 0.0005, f"Unexpected chunk sweep: {chunk_t_stream}")
    check(abs(intent_rate.to(ureg.hertz).magnitude - 2.0) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected intent rate: {intent_rate}")
    check(abs(intent_latency.to(millisecond).magnitude - 335.61) < 5e-3, f"Unexpected intent latency: {intent_latency}")
    check(intent_latency > (1 / chunk_rate), "The intent model's evaluation must exceed the chunk period")
    check(abs(chunk_rate.to(ureg.hertz).magnitude - 20.0) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected chunk rate: {chunk_rate}")
    check(abs(chunk_latency.to(millisecond).magnitude - 40.0) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected chunk latency: {chunk_latency}")
    check(t_stream > (1 / chunk_rate), "The intent sweep alone must exceed the chunk period")
    check(chunk_latency < (1 / chunk_rate), "The chunk policy's inference must fit its own period")
    check(kv_layers == 32 and kv_hidden == 4096, f"Unexpected intent-model shape: {kv_layers} x {kv_hidden}")
    check(visual_tokens == 768 and history_frames == 50, f"Unexpected KV scenario: {visual_tokens}, {history_frames}")
    check(abs(kv_per_token.magnitude - 0.524288) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected KV bytes per token: {kv_per_token}")
    check(abs(kv_history_visual.magnitude - 20.13) < 0.01, f"Unexpected visual KV history: {kv_history_visual}")
    check(abs(kv_history.magnitude - 20.97) < 0.01, f"Unexpected context KV history: {kv_history}")
    check(abs(combined_mem.magnitude - 34.97) < 0.01, f"Unexpected weights plus KV footprint: {combined_mem}")
    check(0.45 < combined_ratio < 0.55, f"Weights plus KV must claim about half the SoC memory: {combined_ratio}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    params_str = fmt_params(params, precision=0)
    chunk_params_str = fmt_params(chunk_params, precision=0)
    bytes_per_param_str = fmt_int(bytes_per_param.magnitude)
    weight_mem_str = fmt_memory(weight_mem, unit=GB, precision=0)
    weight_mem_int4_str = fmt_memory(weight_mem_int4, unit=GB, precision=1)
    chunk_weight_mem_str = fmt_memory(chunk_weight_mem, unit=GB, precision=2)
    b_peak_str = fmt_bandwidth(b_peak, unit=GB / second, precision=0)
    b_sustained_str = fmt_bandwidth(b_sustained, unit=GB / second, precision=1)
    dram_eff_pct_str = fmt_percent(bus_efficiency, precision=0, style="prose")
    t_stream_ms_str = fmt_latency(t_stream, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    f_single_str = fmt_frequency(f_single, unit=ureg.hertz, precision=1)
    chunk_horizon_str = fmt_int(chunk_horizon)
    chunk_step_str = fmt_latency(chunk_step, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    chunk_span_str = fmt_latency(chunk_span, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    tau_step_str = fmt_latency(tau_step, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    chunk_t_stream_str = fmt_latency(chunk_t_stream, unit=millisecond, precision=2)
    intent_rate_str = fmt_frequency(intent_rate, unit=ureg.hertz, precision=0)
    intent_latency_str = fmt_latency(round(intent_latency.to(millisecond).magnitude) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    chunk_rate_str = fmt_frequency(chunk_rate, unit=ureg.hertz, precision=0)
    chunk_latency_str = fmt_latency(chunk_latency, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    kv_layers_str = fmt_int(kv_layers)
    kv_hidden_str = fmt_int(kv_hidden, commas=False)
    cameras_str = fmt_int(cameras)
    patches_per_frame_str = fmt_int(patches_per_frame)
    visual_tokens_str = fmt_int(visual_tokens)
    context_tokens_str = fmt_int(context_tokens)
    history_window_str = fmt_time(history_window, 'second', precision=0)
    history_rate_str = fmt_frequency(history_rate, unit=ureg.hertz, precision=0)
    kv_per_token_str = fmt_memory(kv_per_token, unit=MB, precision=2)
    kv_per_frame_str = fmt_memory(kv_per_frame, unit=MB, precision=1)
    kv_history_visual_str = fmt_memory(kv_history_visual, unit=GB, precision=1)
    kv_per_step_str = fmt_memory(kv_per_step, unit=MB, precision=1)
    kv_history_str = fmt_memory(kv_history, unit=GB, precision=1)
    combined_mem_str = fmt_memory(combined_mem, unit=GB, precision=1)
    soc_mem_gb_str = fmt_memory(soc_mem, unit=GB, precision=1)

    kv_display_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"M_{{\text{{KV}}}} = 2 \times L \times d \times S \times \text{{bytes}} = 2 \times {kv_layers_str} \times {kv_hidden_str} \times S \times 2 \approx {kv_per_token_str} \cdot S"
    )
    tau_step_display_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"\tau_{{\text{{step}}}} = \frac{{t_{{\text{{stream}}}}}}{{H}} = \frac{{{t_stream_ms_str}}}{{{chunk_horizon_str}\text{{ setpoints}}}} \approx {tau_step_str}\text{{ per setpoint}}"
    )
```

::: {#nbk-brain-lpddr5-memory-wall-bottleneck-action-chunking .callout-notebook title="Memory walls, supply, and freshness"}
Can action chunking let a multi-billion-parameter model on an embedded compute module renew proposals as fast as the arm consumes them, or does the machine need a second, smaller proposer?

*1. The weight sweep and retained context.*
\ref{nbk-brain-intent-model-latency} priced one sweep of the intent model's `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.weight_mem_str` of FP16 weights at the `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.b_sustained_str` sustained bandwidth: `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.t_stream_ms_str`, a ceiling of `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.f_single_str` on fresh evaluations. Beyond model weights, retained autoregressive context also occupies KV cache. For a hypothetical multi-camera extension of the backbone, when sensory feeds (e.g., `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.cameras_str` $224 \times 224$ RGB streams) are ingested, each video frame contributes hundreds of visual patch tokens (`{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.cameras_str` $\times$ `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.patches_per_frame_str` $=$ `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.visual_tokens_str` tokens). In the intent model's `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.kv_layers_str`-layer transformer with hidden dimension $d =$ `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.kv_hidden_str`, storing the FP16 Key and Value states consumes `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.kv_per_token_str` per token:
`{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.kv_display_math`
Across one synchronized `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.visual_tokens_str`-token set of camera frames, the KV cache expands by `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.kv_per_frame_str`. This is a full-width, standard multi-head attention estimate; it is not a measured cache footprint for the published OpenVLA checkpoint.

*2. The action chunking amortization.*
Suppose the intent model itself emitted an action chunk of $H =$ `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.chunk_horizon_str` future setpoints ($\Delta t =$ `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.chunk_step_str`, spanning `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.chunk_span_str`) from each forward pass, instead of one action step per DRAM weight sweep.

- Number of weight memory sweeps: 1 sweep (`{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.t_stream_ms_str`).
- A chunk can reuse one backbone evaluation across $H$ future setpoints.
- Amortized weight-sweep time per setpoint (excluding all other inference work):
`{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.tau_step_display_math`

*3. The machine's split.*
Amortization spreads one sweep across more setpoints, but it does not make a fresh proposal arrive sooner. Each new chunk from the intent model would still wait for the compute-bound prefill of its input tokens and the sweeps of its decoder. The selected design therefore divides the work between two models. With INT4 weights the intent model needs about `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.intent_latency_str` per evaluation (\ref{nbk-brain-intent-model-latency}), so it revises its target at `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.intent_rate_str`. A separate `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.chunk_params_str`-parameter chunk policy uses ACT as its size reference and is assumed to be adapted to the mobile manipulator. Its `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.chunk_weight_mem_str` of weights sweep in `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.chunk_t_stream_str`. It proposes base velocity and arm joint targets together at `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.chunk_rate_str` (a `{python} ChunkSchedule.t_replan_str` replanning period), emitting waypoints spaced at $\Delta t =$ `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.chunk_step_str` (a `{python} ChunkSchedule.f_supply_str` supply rate), within a `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.chunk_latency_str` P99 inference target that includes vision, while the drives below interpolate and close their current loops at the rates of @sec-body. The intent model's evaluation lasts several renewal periods; the chunk policy's weight sweep leaves room for the remaining work. That is a candidate architecture, not a measured timing result. Loaded execution must establish the inference target, and a percentile target still permits overruns. The chunk lease that @sec-nervous derives contains a missed renewal.
:::

Retained context adds to the memory pressure that the notebook's first step began to measure. Counting language and proprioception tokens along with the visual patches raises each step to $S \approx$ `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.context_tokens_str` tokens, so at `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.kv_per_token_str` of FP16 key-value state per token each observation step adds `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.kv_per_step_str` of KV cache. Retaining an unpruned `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.history_window_str` historical context window at `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.history_rate_str` would yield `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.kv_history_str` of KV cache. This hypothetical history exceeds the published OpenVLA checkpoint's configured context window; the calculation exposes the storage cost of such an extension, rather than claiming that the checkpoint supports it. Combined with the intent model's `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.weight_mem_str` of weights, this example claims `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.combined_mem_str`, about half of the application processor's `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.soc_mem_gb_str` before runtime overhead, memory that perception, mapping, and the chunk policy also need. Even where memory capacity permits, reading a large cache is further traffic on that same bus (@sec-placement-resource-contention). Bounding retained history therefore serves both capacity and timely renewal. Spatial pooling or cross-attention can reduce context traffic; fixed-horizon action output does not by itself bound the observation history retained by the backbone.

```{python}
#| label: calc-brain-conveyor-chunk-sizing
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CONVEYOR CHUNK SIZING
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: the conveyor-pick paragraph in @sec-brain-cognitive-pipeline
# │ Goal:    size the chunk the mobile manipulator's arm executes against the
# │          mug's drift on the moving conveyor
# │ Show:    the 219 ms tracked evidence horizon; the 90 ms open-loop span
# │          (50 ms replanning period plus 40 ms inference) inside it; the
# │          16-step, 400 ms chunk (25 ms steps since M5, 2026-09-28) as a
# │          supply buffer that would breach the grasp tolerance if executed
# │          to its end
# │ How:     tau_ev = sqrt(2 (r_tol - e_0) / a_slip); open-loop span, h_min, and
# │          chunk span from RM.chunk_schedule; drift = a_slip T^2 / 2
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_latency, fmt_velocity, fmt_acceleration, fmt_length, fmt_int, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class ConveyorChunkSizing:
    """Chunk supply and evidence horizon for the mug on the moving conveyor."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    v_conv = AISLE.v_conveyor  # category: illustrative
    a_slip = AISLE.a_conveyor_slip  # category: illustrative
    r_tol = AISLE.grasp_tolerance  # category: chosen
    e_0 = AISLE.grasp_initial_error  # category: illustrative
    chunk_rate = RM.chunk_rate  # category: chosen
    chunk_latency = RM.chunk_inference_latency  # category: illustrative
    chunk_step = RM.chunk_step  # category: chosen
    chunk_horizon = RM.chunk_horizon  # category: chosen

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    tau_ev = ((2 * (r_tol - e_0) / a_slip) ** 0.5).to(millisecond)
    sched = RM.chunk_schedule  # calc_chunk_renewal_schedule
    chunk_period = sched["renewal_period"]
    open_loop = sched["open_loop_span"]  # renewal period + inference
    h_min = sched["min_supply_setpoints"]  # ceil(open_loop / step)
    chunk_span = sched["chunk_span"]  # H x step
    drift_open_loop = (0.5 * a_slip * open_loop**2).to(millimeter)
    drift_full = (0.5 * a_slip * chunk_span**2).to(millimeter)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(v_conv.to("m/s").magnitude - 0.20) < 1e-9, f"Conveyor speed drifted: {v_conv}")
    check(abs(tau_ev.magnitude - 219.09) < 5e-3, f"Tracked evidence horizon drifted: {tau_ev}")
    check(abs(chunk_period.magnitude - 50.0) < 1e-9, f"Chunk period drifted: {chunk_period}")
    check(abs(open_loop.magnitude - 90.0) < 1e-9, f"Open-loop span drifted: {open_loop}")
    check(open_loop < tau_ev, "The open-loop span must sit inside the evidence horizon")
    check(h_min == 4, f"Minimum supply horizon drifted: {h_min}")
    check(h_min * chunk_step >= open_loop, "The minimum supply must bridge the open-loop span")
    check(chunk_horizon == 16, f"Chunk horizon drifted: {chunk_horizon}")
    check(abs(chunk_span.magnitude - 400.0) < 1e-9, f"Chunk span drifted: {chunk_span}")
    check(chunk_span > tau_ev, "The full chunk must outlast the evidence horizon (buffer, not plan)")
    check(e_0 + drift_full > r_tol, "Executing the whole chunk open-loop must breach the grasp tolerance")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    v_conv_str = fmt_velocity(v_conv, unit="m/s", precision=2)
    a_slip_str = fmt_acceleration(a_slip, precision=2)
    r_tol_str = fmt_length(r_tol, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    e_0_str = fmt_length(e_0, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    tau_ev_rounded = round(tau_ev.magnitude) * millisecond  # whole-ms display; the guard pins 219.09 ms
    tau_ev_str = fmt_latency(tau_ev_rounded, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    chunk_period_str = fmt_latency(chunk_period, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    chunk_latency_str = fmt_latency(chunk_latency, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    open_loop_str = fmt_latency(open_loop, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    h_min_str = fmt_int(h_min)
    chunk_horizon_str = fmt_int(chunk_horizon)
    chunk_step_str = fmt_latency(chunk_step, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    chunk_span_str = fmt_latency(chunk_span, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    drift_open_loop_str = fmt_length(drift_open_loop, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    drift_full_str = fmt_length(drift_full, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
```

The split fixes how often each proposer renews. The moving target fixes how long each renewal stays true. In the illustrative conveyor calculation, the mobile manipulator's arm takes the mug from a conveyor moving at `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.v_conv_str`, and each chunk must be executed without letting the mug drift out of reach. Untracked, the belt's steady motion would use up the margin $r_{\text{tol}} - e_0$ between the grasp tolerance and the handle estimate's initial error $e_0$ within the freshness deadline $e_{\max}/v_{\max}$ of @sec-body-measurement-freshness, with $e_{\max} = r_{\text{tol}} - e_0$. A tracker that follows the mug removes that steady motion, but residual slip can still accelerate the target at `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.a_slip_str`, so a segment executed open-loop for a time $T$ drifts by $\frac{1}{2} a_{\text{slip}} T^2$. Added to the `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.e_0_str` initial error $e_0$, that drift reaches the `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.r_tol_str` grasp tolerance after the tracked evidence horizon $\tau_{\text{ev}} = \sqrt{2 (r_{\text{tol}} - e_0) / a_{\text{slip}}} \approx$ `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.tau_ev_str`. The chunk policy replans every `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.chunk_period_str` and is assumed to finish within `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.chunk_latency_str`. Before additional handoff delays, this schedule gives a maximum evidence age at replacement of `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.open_loop_str` and residual drift of `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.drift_open_loop_str`, within the tracked evidence horizon. An overrun ends this assumption; the chunk lease then limits continued execution.

That open-loop span also sets the minimum supply, because a chunk shorter than `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.h_min_str` setpoints would leave the arm waiting for its successor. The machine's chunk carries `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.chunk_horizon_str` setpoints at `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.chunk_step_str` spacing, `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.chunk_span_str` of motion, longer than the tracked evidence horizon; executed open-loop to its end, it would drift `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.drift_full_str`, past the tolerance. The unexecuted tail is therefore a supply buffer, not permission to finish the predicted trajectory (@fig-03-chunk-supply-horizon). If renewal stops, any further prefix remains eligible only while its evidence and active chunk lease remain valid. @Sec-nervous-cadences derives the lease and accounts for the handoff delays before that buffer runs out. Overlapping chunks and temporal ensembling then blend the executed motion across each renewal.

::: {#fig-03-chunk-supply-horizon fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Chunk supply against the evidence horizon**: Time runs from the capture that the first chunk is computed from. The chunk policy renews every `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.chunk_period_str` and needs `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.chunk_latency_str` per evaluation, so each chunk is in force for one renewal period and is replaced when its evidence is `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.open_loop_str` old. The first chunk predicts `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.chunk_span_str` of setpoints, but the tracked mug stays within the grasp tolerance only for the `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.tau_ev_str` evidence horizon; the hatched tail is supply that keeps the setpoint stream full if renewal slips, not permission to execute it." fig-alt="Timing strip with five lanes on a shared millisecond axis from 0 to about 440. Capture ticks every 50 milliseconds; inference bars 40 milliseconds long starting at each capture; a lane showing chunks 0 to 3 each in force for 50 milliseconds starting at 40; the first chunk's span from 40 to 440 split into an executed segment to 90, a segment labeled evidence still valid to a red dashed line at 219, and a hatched segment labeled buffer, not permission to 440; and setpoint ticks every 25 milliseconds. Brackets above mark the 25 millisecond step, the 50 millisecond renewal, and the 90 millisecond age at replacement."}

```{python}
#| label: fig-03-chunk-supply-horizon
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CHUNK SUPPLY AGAINST THE EVIDENCE HORIZON (FIGURE)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-03-chunk-supply-horizon, after the conveyor chunk-sizing

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

from mlsysim.fmt import check

_strip = viz.chunk_renewal_strip(RM, evidence_horizon=ConveyorChunkSizing.tau_ev)

# ┌── 3. GUARD (the strip draws the same schedule the prose prints) ───────────
check(RM.chunk_schedule["open_loop_span"] == ConveyorChunkSizing.open_loop, "Strip and prose disagree on the age at replacement.")
check(RM.chunk_schedule["chunk_span"] == ConveyorChunkSizing.chunk_span, "Strip and prose disagree on the chunk span.")
check(
    ConveyorChunkSizing.open_loop < ConveyorChunkSizing.tau_ev < ConveyorChunkSizing.chunk_span,
```

↪ Bounded action chunk proposals are filtered against forward-invariant barriers in @sec-enforcement-safe-sets-conditional-permission.

Under the stated assumptions, the conveyor calculation supplies the quantities needed to connect cognition to physical permission. One chunk covers `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.chunk_span_str` of motion, a new chunk takes up to `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.chunk_latency_str`, and the evidence stays within the stated grasp tolerance for about `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.tau_ev_str`. The Nervous System must combine these proposer limits with the body's measured limits to establish its handoff record. That requires more information than a trajectory tensor alone. Timely delivery and usable evidence bound how long a proposal can remain eligible; they do not establish that the proposed grasp was correct.

### Handing intent to the chunk policy {#sec-brain-proposer-interface}

```{python}
#| label: calc-brain-proposer-interface
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ AGE OF THE INTENT MODEL'S TARGET ON ARRIVAL
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-brain-proposer-interface and @tbl-03-state-of-practice
# │ Goal:    show that a target pose from one intent evaluation is already
# │          older than the conveyor's tracked evidence horizon when it arrives
# │ Show:    336 ms evaluation > 219 ms tau_ev, so a tracker must renew the pose
# │ How:     IntentModelLatency.t_int4 against ConveyorChunkSizing.tau_ev
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Embodied
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_latency, fmt_params, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

class ProposerInterface:
    """Age of the intent model's target pose against the tracked evidence horizon."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    t_intent = IntentModelLatency.t_int4  # category: derived (calc_vla_inference_latency)
    tau_ev = ConveyorChunkSizing.tau_ev  # category: derived (conveyor slip model)
    chunk_params = RM.chunk_model.parameters  # category: datasheet (ACT)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    age_ratio = (t_intent / tau_ev).to("dimensionless").magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(t_intent > tau_ev, "The intent target must be staler on arrival than the evidence horizon")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    chunk_params_str = fmt_params(chunk_params, precision=0)
```

The split between a slow semantic model and a fast visuomotor policy is not peculiar to this machine. Helix runs a `{python} StateOfPractice.helix_s2_params_str`-parameter vision-language model at `{python} StateOfPractice.helix_s2_lo_num_str` to `{python} StateOfPractice.helix_s2_hi_str` above an `{python} StateOfPractice.helix_s1_params_str`-parameter policy at `{python} StateOfPractice.helix_s1_rate_str` [@figureai2025helix], and GR00T N1 runs its vision-language model at `{python} StateOfPractice.gr00t_s2_rate_str` above a flow-matching transformer at `{python} StateOfPractice.gr00t_s1_rate_str` [@bjorck2025gr00t]. @Tbl-03-state-of-practice collects these and other published designs. Their rates bracket the machine's own `{python} IntentModelLatency.rate_str` and `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.chunk_rate_str`. What separates them is less their rates than what the slow model hands the fast one, and that choice decides what the permission path can check.

Three kinds of interface are in use. The first is a *latent vector*. Helix's slow model passes a single continuous latent that conditions the fast policy [@figureai2025helix], and GR00T N1's policy attends to token embeddings taken from an intermediate layer of its vision-language model [@bjorck2025gr00t]. A latent is trained end to end, carries whatever the fast policy finds useful, and costs no decoding. The second is a *language subtask*. $\pi_{0.5}$ first predicts the next subtask as text and then generates actions conditioned on it [@black2025pi05], and the orchestrating model of Gemini Robotics 1.5 sends its action model natural-language step instructions [@geminirobotics2025gemini15]. The third is a *geometric target*: Gemini Robotics-ER predicts points, two- and three-dimensional boxes, trajectories, and grasps, each with coordinates in the scene [@geminirobotics2025].

The permission path can check only a claim it can compare with its own evidence, and the three interfaces differ exactly there. A latent vector means something only to the network that reads it. No independent checker can tell whether it refers to the mug or to the photograph of a mug on a carton (@sec-brain-semantic-hallucinations), and it carries no position that could age against the evidence horizon $\tau_{\text{ev}}$. A text subtask can be checked against the task predicates the permission path has admitted, but "pick up the mug" names no location, so it can be neither compared with measured depth nor aged against drift. A geometric target allows both checks. It can be compared with calibrated depth and keep-out geometry, and aged from the capture time of the frame it came from. Only this interface lets an intent lease be enforced, because the lease grants a grounded target (@sec-intent-lease). With a latent or a text interface, the permission path can still check each chunk's motion under the chunk lease, but the intent behind that motion goes unchecked.

The mobile manipulator therefore has its intent model emit a target: a position, an orientation, and a gripper command, the same seven values OpenVLA decodes as a step of motion, together with the capture time of the frame it read. The timing shows why that target cannot stand alone. One evaluation takes `{python} IntentModelLatency.total_int4_str`, longer than the `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.tau_ev_str` tracked evidence horizon of the conveyor pick, so the target pose is stale before it arrives. The intent model names which object to take and approximately where; a tracker that re-measures the mug on every frame supplies the fresh pose that the `{python} ProposerInterface.chunk_params_str`-parameter chunk policy aims at and that the intent lease ages against (@sec-intent-lease).

The geometric bottleneck costs capability. A target pose cannot say how to fold a shirt or where to regrasp a cable, information a latent carries without a schema, so a checkable interface limits the tasks a single target can express. The machine accepts that limit in exchange for an intent the permission path can refuse. The same reasoning applies one level down to the chunk policy's action space. Joint targets can be checked directly against joint limits and end-effector poses against workspace keep-out regions, which is why the proposal payload of @sec-brain-proposer-information carries both.
